skills.name: World Geography
skills.description: From reading a map to the mountains, rivers, climates and peoples of every continent.

skills.name: Ancient Rome
skills.description: From a village on the Tiber to an empire around the Mediterranean, and why it still shapes our laws, words and cities.

skills.name: How Money Works
skills.description: From barter and coins to banks, markets, inflation and trade: the ideas behind every price you pay.

skills.name: Astronomy
skills.description: From your cosmic address to the edge of the observable universe: the flagship 1–100 tree.

concepts.title: The Battle of Actium
concepts.description: Octavian’s fleet under Agrippa defeated Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BCE, leaving Octavian sole master of Rome.

concepts.title: The Battle of Adrianople
concepts.description: In 378 CE Goths who had crossed the Danube destroyed a Roman army and killed the emperor Valens.

concepts.title: Virgil and the Aeneid
concepts.description: Virgil’s epic of the Trojan Aeneas gave Rome a founding poem and Augustus a heroic ancestor.

concepts.title: Antony and Cleopatra
concepts.description: Mark Antony ruled the East in alliance with Cleopatra, giving Octavian a foreign enemy to fight.

concepts.title: Aqueducts
concepts.description: Gravity carried water along gentle slopes, mostly underground, to supply Roman cities.

concepts.title: Attila and the Huns
concepts.description: Attila extorted gold from the East, was stopped in Gaul in 451 and turned back from Italy in 452.

concepts.title: Augustus and the Principate
concepts.description: Augustus ruled as princeps, keeping the Republic’s forms while holding the real power.

concepts.title: The Roman baths
concepts.description: Heated public baths with hot, warm and cold rooms were cheap social centers for all classes.

concepts.title: Bread and circuses
concepts.description: Free grain and public games kept Rome’s crowds fed, entertained and loyal to the rulers who paid.

concepts.title: Caesar in Gaul
concepts.description: Caesar conquered Gaul in 58–50 BCE, beat Vercingetorix at Alesia and gained a loyal veteran army.

concepts.title: Caligula
concepts.description: A young emperor who began popular and became autocratic; much of his legend comes from hostile writers.

concepts.title: Cannae
concepts.description: In 216 BCE Hannibal encircled and destroyed a larger Roman army, yet Rome refused to make peace.

concepts.title: The destruction of Carthage
concepts.description: Urged on by Cato, Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE and made its land the province of Africa.

concepts.title: Carthage
concepts.description: A Phoenician trading city in North Africa that ruled the western Mediterranean’s seas and clashed with Rome over Sicily.

concepts.title: The empire of 395
concepts.description: By 395 the empire was Christian, ruled by distant monarchs, split in two and defended partly by Germanic allies.

concepts.title: Chariot racing
concepts.description: Rome’s most popular spectacle, raced by four color factions at the vast Circus Maximus.

concepts.title: A Christian empire
concepts.description: Under Theodosius, Christianity became the official religion and the old cults were shut down.

concepts.title: Cicero and Catiline
concepts.description: The great orator, consul in 63 BCE, exposed Catiline’s plot and executed conspirators without trial.

concepts.title: Roman citizenship
concepts.description: Citizenship spread from Rome to Italy and the provinces until Caracalla extended it to almost all free people in 212.

concepts.title: Life in the city of Rome
concepts.description: A city of perhaps a million, where most lived in crowded insulae and public life centered on the Forum.

concepts.title: Augustus rebuilds Rome
concepts.description: Augustus and Agrippa filled Rome with temples and public works that advertised his piety and his peace.

concepts.title: Cincinnatus and civic virtue
concepts.description: The Roman ideal of the citizen who serves in a crisis and then gives power back.

concepts.title: Claudius and Britain
concepts.description: An emperor few took seriously, Claudius launched the conquest of Britain in 43 CE.

concepts.title: The Conflict of the Orders
concepts.description: Plebeians won political rights from the patricians over about two centuries, using walkouts as leverage.

concepts.title: Conquering Italy
concepts.description: Through the Samnite Wars, roads like the Via Appia and a network of allies, Rome came to control Italy by about 264 BCE.

concepts.title: Constantine
concepts.description: Constantine won at the Milvian Bridge, granted Christians tolerance and called the Council of Nicaea.

concepts.title: Constantinople
concepts.description: Constantine’s new Rome on the Bosporus, closer to the frontiers, lasted as a capital for over a thousand years.

concepts.title: Consuls
concepts.description: Two consuls, elected each year, led Rome and its armies; each could block the other.

concepts.title: Diocletian and the Tetrarchy
concepts.description: Diocletian ended the crisis with rule by four emperors, smaller provinces and a split between East and West.

concepts.title: How Rome began
concepts.description: A strategic river site, merging Latin villages, Etruscan influence and founding legends together explain early Rome.

concepts.title: Rome’s first villages
concepts.description: Archaeology shows Latin hilltop villages from about the 8th century BCE that merged into a town around a drained valley, the Forum.

concepts.title: The Eastern Roman Empire
concepts.description: The Greek-speaking “Byzantine” empire called itself Roman and lasted until 1453.

concepts.title: The Etruscans
concepts.description: Rome’s powerful northern neighbors, whose kings, symbols and rituals shaped early Rome.

concepts.title: Everyday Rome
concepts.description: Cramped homes pushed life into public spaces, bound together by patrons, gods, bread and games.

concepts.title: Fabius the Delayer
concepts.description: Fabius wore Hannibal down by avoiding battle; Rome’s loyal allies starved him of reinforcements.

concepts.title: 476: the last western emperor
concepts.description: Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 CE; historians debate how much actually changed.

concepts.title: The end of the kings
concepts.description: Tarquin the Proud was expelled in 509 BCE after the Lucretia scandal, and Romans swore never to have a king again.

concepts.title: The first Christians
concepts.description: A Jewish movement from Judaea spread through the empire’s cities, carried by its roads, peace and Greek.

concepts.title: The First Punic War
concepts.description: Rome built a navy, used the corvus boarding bridge, and won Sicily, its first province, in 241 BCE.

concepts.title: The First Triumvirate
concepts.description: The 60 BCE alliance of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus, which broke apart after Julia’s and Crassus’s deaths.

concepts.title: The Five Good Emperors
concepts.description: From 96 to 180 CE, emperors chosen by adoption gave Rome its most stable era; Commodus ended it.

concepts.title: The Flavians and the Colosseum
concepts.description: Vespasian and his sons ruled from 69 to 96 CE and built the Colosseum on Nero’s palace grounds.

concepts.title: Romulus and Remus
concepts.description: Rome’s founding legend: twins raised by a she-wolf, a fratricide, and a city named for Romulus.

concepts.title: The Year of the Four Emperors
concepts.description: In 69 CE four men held power in turn, each backed by an army; Vespasian won and founded the Flavian dynasty.

concepts.title: Life on the frontier
concepts.description: Forts, auxiliaries and the towns beside them held the limes, as the Vindolanda letters reveal.

concepts.title: The Gallic sack of Rome
concepts.description: Around 390 BCE Gauls under Brennus sacked Rome; afterwards the city built a great stone wall.

concepts.title: Gladiators
concepts.description: Mostly enslaved or condemned fighters in set types; many bouts ended without a death, and the thumb signal is uncertain.

concepts.title: The Gracchi
concepts.description: Two tribunes who tried to give land to poor citizens and were killed, bringing violence into Roman politics.

concepts.title: Hadrian and his wall
concepts.description: Hadrian stopped expanding, toured the frontiers and fortified them, most famously in northern Britain.

concepts.title: Hannibal crosses the Alps
concepts.description: In 218 BCE Hannibal marched from Spain over the Alps with elephants to invade Italy, starting the Second Punic War.

concepts.title: How Rome held an empire
concepts.description: Roads, citizenship, law, trade and a shared army bound the empire together, not force alone.

concepts.title: The Ides of March
concepts.description: Made dictator for life, Caesar was assassinated on 15 March 44 BCE, but his death did not save the Republic.

concepts.title: Julian the Apostate
concepts.description: Constantine’s nephew tried to restore the old gods, but died in Persia after less than two years.

concepts.title: The Julian calendar
concepts.description: Caesar’s 365-day calendar with a leap year; July and August were renamed for Caesar and Augustus.

concepts.title: Latin and its descendants
concepts.description: Rome’s language spread west, became the Romance languages and still fills English.

concepts.title: Rome in our words, calendars and cities
concepts.description: Roman towns, grids, columns, mottoes and months still shape the world.

concepts.title: Rome in our laws and governments
concepts.description: Senates, vetoes, capitols, balanced constitutions and civil law all come from Rome.

concepts.title: The legion
concepts.description: Citizen soldiers in flexible maniples and three lines, armed with the gladius and pilum.

concepts.title: Marius and the army
concepts.description: Marius opened the legions to the landless poor, who then looked to their generals rather than the Senate.

concepts.title: Master of the Mediterranean
concepts.description: By 146 BCE the Punic and Macedonian wars had made Rome the Mediterranean’s dominant power, ruling provinces through governors.

concepts.title: How the Republic worked
concepts.description: Consuls, Senate and assemblies each checked the others, a “mixed constitution” admired by Polybius.

concepts.title: Money and trade
concepts.description: Silver coins carried the emperor’s face; amphorae carried wine, oil and garum across a connected Mediterranean.

concepts.title: Nero and the Great Fire
concepts.description: Nero, emperor from 54 CE, blamed the Christians for the fire of 64 CE; his death in 68 CE ended Augustus’ line.

concepts.title: Octavian, Caesar’s heir
concepts.description: Caesar’s adopted heir used his name, the Second Triumvirate and victory at Philippi to build his power.

concepts.title: The Pantheon
concepts.description: Hadrian’s temple has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, lit by a single open oculus.

concepts.title: The Pax Romana
concepts.description: About 200 years of relative peace, from Augustus to Marcus Aurelius, in which trade and cities flourished.

concepts.title: Persecution
concepts.description: Local and sporadic at first, persecution became empire-wide under Decius and harshest under Diocletian.

concepts.title: Pompeii and Vesuvius
concepts.description: The eruption of 79 CE buried Pompeii and preserved an ordinary Roman town for historians.

concepts.title: Pompey the Great
concepts.description: A general of extraordinary commands who swept the pirates from the sea and reorganized the East.

concepts.title: Running the provinces
concepts.description: Governors, taxes and local elites ran a vast empire with very few Roman officials.

concepts.title: The Roman Republic
concepts.description: A state run by elected officials with limited terms, the “Senate and People of Rome.”

concepts.title: From Republic to Empire
concepts.description: Violence and loyal armies turned the Republic into one-man rule that kept republican forms.

concepts.title: The arc of Roman history
concepts.description: From 753 BCE to 1453 CE, one thread runs through it: whoever held the army held the state.

concepts.title: Roman concrete
concepts.description: Lime and volcanic ash made a concrete that set underwater, shaped domes and has lasted two thousand years.

concepts.title: How we know about Rome
concepts.description: Historians weigh biased texts against inscriptions, coins and archaeology.

concepts.title: The Roman family
concepts.description: The paterfamilias held legal power over his descendants; the familia included the whole household.

concepts.title: What Romans ate
concepts.description: Grain, oil and wine for most; reclining banquets for the rich; garum fish sauce for everyone.

concepts.title: The seven kings
concepts.description: Tradition counts seven kings from 753 to 509 BCE, chosen with the approval of the Senate and people.

concepts.title: Roman law
concepts.description: From the Twelve Tables to Justinian’s code, Roman law became the base of the world’s civil law systems.

concepts.title: Roman religion
concepts.description: Correct ritual kept the peace of the gods, from household spirits to Jupiter’s temple, Vesta’s fire and augury.

concepts.title: Roman roads
concepts.description: A vast network of layered, drained, straight roads built for the army and used by everyone.

concepts.title: Roman women
concepts.description: Women could own property and wield influence, but could not vote or hold office.

concepts.title: Rome turns east
concepts.description: Rome defeated Macedon and came to dominate Greece, while Greek culture transformed Rome.

concepts.title: Rome’s three eras
concepts.description: Roman history runs from the Kingdom to the Republic (509 BCE) to the Empire (27 BCE); the West fell in 476 CE and the East in 1453.

concepts.title: An empire around a sea
concepts.description: At its height Rome ruled every coast of the Mediterranean, which Romans called “our sea.”

concepts.title: Seven hills and a river
concepts.description: Rome grew at a crossing of the Tiber on a trade route, on defensible hills, with Ostia as its port.

concepts.title: Crossing the Rubicon
concepts.description: In 49 BCE Caesar led his army across the Rubicon into Italy, starting a civil war he won at Pharsalus.

concepts.title: The sack of Rome, 410
concepts.description: Alaric’s Visigoths sacked Rome in 410 CE, a shock that led Augustine to write The City of God.

concepts.title: Scipio and Zama
concepts.description: Scipio took Spain, invaded Africa and beat Hannibal at Zama in 202 BCE, ending the Second Punic War.

concepts.title: The Senate
concepts.description: Former magistrates, usually for life, whose advice on war, diplomacy and money was almost always followed.

concepts.title: Slavery in Rome
concepts.description: Enslaved people did every kind of work; many were freed, and freed slaves of citizens became citizens.

concepts.title: Spartacus
concepts.description: A gladiator who led a huge slave revolt from 73 BCE until Crassus crushed it in 71 BCE.

concepts.title: Sulla
concepts.description: The first general to march on Rome; as dictator without a time limit he killed enemies by proscription.

concepts.title: The Teutoburg Forest
concepts.description: In 9 CE Arminius destroyed three legions under Varus, and Rome settled on the Rhine as its frontier.

concepts.title: The Crisis of the Third Century
concepts.description: From 235 to 284 CE, rapid-fire emperors, invasions, plague and inflation nearly broke the empire apart.

concepts.title: Tiberius and succession
concepts.description: Augustus’ adopted stepson ruled from 14 to 37 CE; with no law of succession, every heir was a gamble.

concepts.title: Trajan
concepts.description: The first emperor from outside Italy conquered Dacia and brought the empire to its greatest extent in 117 CE.

concepts.title: Tribunes of the plebs
concepts.description: Plebeian officials who could veto any magistrate and who were sacrosanct.

concepts.title: The Twelve Tables
concepts.description: Rome’s first written laws, displayed in the Forum around 450 BCE so everyone could know them.

concepts.title: Why did Rome fall?
concepts.description: Invasions, civil wars and lost revenue broke the West; some historians prefer to speak of transformation.

concepts.title: The sky as the first calendar
concepts.description: Ancient cultures tracked the Sun, Moon and stars to mark seasons, plan farming and hold ceremonies.

concepts.title: Andromeda, our big neighbor
concepts.description: Andromeda is the nearest large spiral galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away.

concepts.title: The Apollo Moon landings
concepts.description: Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon during six Apollo landings between 1969 and 1972, bringing back 382 kg of samples.

concepts.title: Asterisms: patterns within constellations
concepts.description: Familiar star patterns like the Big Dipper are asterisms, not official constellations.

concepts.title: The asteroid belt
concepts.description: A wide ring of rocky and metallic asteroids between Mars and Jupiter that never formed a planet.

concepts.title: The astronomical unit
concepts.description: The average Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km, is the yardstick of the solar system.

concepts.title: The atmosphere gets in the way
concepts.description: Earth’s moving air blurs starlight (stars twinkle) and blocks much of the spectrum, which is why some telescopes go to space.

concepts.title: The Big Bang
concepts.description: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in a hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since.

concepts.title: Binary stars
concepts.description: Many stars orbit partners; watching their orbits lets astronomers weigh stars.

concepts.title: Black holes
concepts.description: A region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape; formed when very massive stars collapse.

concepts.title: Stars that never set
concepts.description: Stars close to the celestial pole circle it and, from mid-northern latitudes, never dip below the horizon.

concepts.title: Galaxy clusters and gravitational lenses
concepts.description: Galaxies gather in clusters whose gravity bends and magnifies the light of galaxies behind them.

concepts.title: The cosmic microwave background
concepts.description: The Big Bang’s leftover light, released about 380,000 years after it began and stretched into microwaves by the expansion.

concepts.title: Comets
concepts.description: Comets are icy bodies that grow a glowing head and tails when they near the Sun; their tails always point away from it.

concepts.title: Constellation stars aren’t neighbors
concepts.description: Stars in the same constellation are usually at very different distances and only line up from our viewpoint.

concepts.title: What constellations are
concepts.description: Constellations are patterns of stars and, officially, 88 regions that together cover the whole sky.

concepts.title: Futures of the Sun, Earth and universe
concepts.description: Earth’s axis will point away from Polaris, the Sun will brighten and swell, galaxies will merge, and accelerating expansion will carry distant galaxies from view.

concepts.title: From atoms to galaxies
concepts.description: Big Bang gas formed stars; stars forged heavier elements and returned them to space, where they built new stars, planets and people.

concepts.title: The cosmic web
concepts.description: On the largest scales, galaxies form a web of filaments and sheets around vast, nearly empty voids.

concepts.title: Dark energy
concepts.description: In 1998 astronomers found the expansion of the universe is speeding up; the unknown cause is called dark energy.

concepts.title: Dark matter
concepts.description: Galaxies spin too fast for their visible matter; an unseen mass, dark matter, outweighs ordinary matter about five to one.

concepts.title: Dwarf planets and Pluto
concepts.description: In 2006 the IAU defined a planet as clearing its orbital neighborhood; Pluto doesn’t, so it’s a dwarf planet.

concepts.title: A year is one orbit
concepts.description: Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once, moving at about 30 km per second.

concepts.title: What protects life on Earth
concepts.description: Earth’s magnetic field deflects charged particles from the Sun, and its atmosphere and ozone layer shield the surface.

concepts.title: Earth’s spin makes day and night
concepts.description: Earth rotates on its axis about once every 24 hours; the side facing the Sun has day.

concepts.title: Earth is the third planet
concepts.description: Our solar system has eight planets; Earth is the third from the Sun.

concepts.title: The 400× coincidence
concepts.description: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, so they look the same size.

concepts.title: Solar vs lunar eclipses
concepts.description: A solar eclipse is the Moon blocking the Sun; a lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.

concepts.title: The ecliptic
concepts.description: The Sun’s yearly path across the sky; the Moon and planets stay close to it because the solar system is flat.

concepts.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
concepts.description: Visible light is one small band of a spectrum that runs from radio waves to gamma rays; all of it is light traveling at the same speed.

concepts.title: Eratosthenes measures Earth
concepts.description: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes compared noon shadows in two Egyptian cities to estimate Earth’s circumference.

concepts.title: Escape velocity
concepts.description: To leave Earth completely, a spacecraft must reach about 11.2 km per second.

concepts.title: The event horizon
concepts.description: The boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can return; the EHT imaged a black hole’s shadow in 2019.

concepts.title: How we know what we know
concepts.description: Most astronomical knowledge comes from reading the light and other signals the universe sends us.

concepts.title: Finding exoplanets
concepts.description: Most exoplanets are found by the dips in starlight they cause (transits) or the wobble they give their stars.

concepts.title: The first stars and galaxies
concepts.description: After the cosmic dark ages, the first stars, made of only hydrogen and helium, lit up within a few hundred million years.

concepts.title: Galaxy collisions
concepts.description: Galaxies collide and merge; the Milky Way and Andromeda are expected to merge in about 4.5 billion years.

concepts.title: Kinds of galaxies
concepts.description: Galaxies come as spirals, ellipticals and irregulars, a scheme Edwin Hubble introduced.

concepts.title: Galileo’s telescope discoveries
concepts.description: From 1609–1610 Galileo turned a telescope to the sky and found evidence that not everything circles Earth.

concepts.title: The Earth-centered model
concepts.description: For centuries, most scholars placed a motionless Earth at the center, with Ptolemy’s model using small circles (epicycles) to fit planetary motion.

concepts.title: Why an Earth-centered view made sense
concepts.description: We don’t feel Earth moving, and no one could detect stars shifting as Earth orbited.

concepts.title: Gas giants and ice giants
concepts.description: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.

concepts.title: Gravitational waves
concepts.description: Ripples in spacetime predicted by Einstein and first detected by LIGO in 2015 from merging black holes.

concepts.title: The habitable zone
concepts.description: The range of distances from a star where a planet could have liquid water on its surface; closer in for dim stars.

concepts.title: The Sun-centered model
concepts.description: Copernicus placed the Sun at the center, with Earth as one of the planets orbiting it.

concepts.title: The heliosphere
concepts.description: The solar wind blows a bubble around the solar system; Voyager 1 crossed its edge in 2012.

concepts.title: Helium was found in the Sun first
concepts.description: Helium was discovered in the Sun’s spectrum in 1868, before it was found on Earth; its name comes from the Greek word for Sun.

concepts.title: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram
concepts.description: A chart of stars’ luminosity against temperature; most fall on a diagonal band, the main sequence.

concepts.title: Hubble’s expanding universe
concepts.description: Hubble showed that other galaxies lie far beyond the Milky Way and that they are moving away from us, faster the farther they are.

concepts.title: The Hubble Space Telescope
concepts.description: Launched in 1990, Hubble orbits above the atmosphere and has made some of astronomy’s sharpest images.

concepts.title: Uranus and Neptune up close
concepts.description: Uranus is tipped on its side; Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system; methane makes both blue.

concepts.title: Infrared astronomy
concepts.description: Infrared light passes through dust, revealing hidden star birth, and captures light from the most distant galaxies.

concepts.title: Jupiter outweighs every other planet combined
concepts.description: Jupiter is the largest planet and has more than twice the mass of all the others put together.

concepts.title: Jupiter’s storms and moons
concepts.description: Jupiter’s Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth; its four large moons are worlds in their own right.

concepts.title: Kepler’s laws
concepts.description: Planets orbit in ellipses, sweep equal areas in equal times, and take longer to orbit the farther out they are.

concepts.title: The Kuiper Belt
concepts.description: A vast ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, home to Pluto and the source of many comets.

concepts.title: Why leap years exist
concepts.description: The extra quarter-day in each orbit adds up, so the calendar adds a day about every four years.

concepts.title: A light-year is a distance
concepts.description: A light-year is how far light travels in a year: about 9.46 trillion km.

concepts.title: The Local Group
concepts.description: The Milky Way belongs to the Local Group, dominated by the Milky Way and Andromeda, with dozens of smaller galaxies.

concepts.title: Brightness versus luminosity
concepts.description: How bright a star looks depends on its true output and its distance; brightness fades with the square of distance.

concepts.title: Lunar craters
concepts.description: The Moon’s craters were blasted out by impacts and survive for billions of years because the Moon has no air, water or plate tectonics to erase them.

concepts.title: The Moon’s dark “seas”
concepts.description: The dark patches on the Moon are maria: huge plains of ancient solidified lava, not water.

concepts.title: A star’s mass sets its life
concepts.description: On the main sequence, more massive stars are hotter and brighter but burn out far faster.

concepts.title: Why Mars is red
concepts.description: Mars looks red because iron oxide, better known as rust, coats its dust and rocks.

concepts.title: Mars once had water
concepts.description: Dry river valleys and lake beds show that liquid water once flowed on Mars; today its water is frozen.

concepts.title: Mercury: extremes without air
concepts.description: The smallest planet and closest to the Sun, Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so it swings from scorching days to frigid nights.

concepts.title: Meteoroids, meteors and meteorites
concepts.description: A meteoroid is space debris, a meteor is its streak of light in our sky, and a meteorite is what reaches the ground.

concepts.title: The Milky Way is our galaxy
concepts.description: The Sun is one of more than a hundred billion stars in the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy.

concepts.title: The Milky Way is ~100,000 light-years across
concepts.description: Our galaxy is about 100,000 light-years from edge to edge.

concepts.title: The structure of the Milky Way
concepts.description: A barred spiral with a central bulge, spiral arms, and a halo; the Sun orbits the center about every 230 million years.

concepts.title: The giant-impact origin of the Moon
concepts.description: The leading explanation is that the Moon formed from debris after a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth.

concepts.title: What causes Moon phases
concepts.description: Phases show how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces us; the cycle takes about 29.5 days.

concepts.title: Evidence from Moon rocks
concepts.description: Moon rocks are chemically very similar to Earth’s mantle and the Moon has only a small iron core, consistent with the giant impact.

concepts.title: The Moon always shows us the same face
concepts.description: The Moon is tidally locked: it rotates once per orbit, so the same side always faces Earth.

concepts.title: Each kind of light tells a different story
concepts.description: Astronomers combine radio, infrared, visible, ultraviolet and X-ray views, each revealing different objects.

concepts.title: The nearest star after the Sun
concepts.description: Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away, is the closest star to the Sun.

concepts.title: Neptune found by mathematics
concepts.description: Irregularities in Uranus’s orbit led astronomers to predict Neptune’s position; it was found there in 1846.

concepts.title: Neutron stars
concepts.description: The collapsed core left by a supernova: about 20 km across yet more massive than the Sun.

concepts.title: Newton’s law of gravity
concepts.description: One force, universal gravitation, explains falling objects, the Moon’s orbit and Kepler’s laws.

concepts.title: The night sky changes with the seasons
concepts.description: As Earth orbits the Sun, the night side faces different directions in space, so different constellations are visible in different seasons.

concepts.title: The observable universe
concepts.description: We can only see as far as light has traveled since the Big Bang; expansion makes that region about 93 billion light-years across.

concepts.title: Ocean worlds
concepts.description: Some icy moons, like Europa and Enceladus, hide oceans of liquid water beneath their ice, kept liquid by tidal heating.

concepts.title: The Oort Cloud
concepts.description: A vast, distant shell of icy bodies thought to surround the solar system, the source of long-period comets.

concepts.title: The big open questions
concepts.description: Dark matter, dark energy, the Hubble tension, what came before the Big Bang, and life elsewhere remain unsolved.

concepts.title: An orbit is falling around
concepts.description: A spacecraft in orbit is falling toward Earth but moving sideways so fast that it keeps missing.

concepts.title: Measuring star distances with parallax
concepts.description: Nearby stars shift slightly as Earth orbits; the smaller the shift, the farther the star.

concepts.title: Planets wander against the stars
concepts.description: Planets shift position against the background stars from night to night; “planet” comes from the Greek for wanderer.

concepts.title: The North Star marks north
concepts.description: Polaris sits almost directly above Earth’s North Pole, so it barely moves and marks north.

concepts.title: Earth’s wobble changes the pole star
concepts.description: Earth’s axis slowly wobbles over about 26,000 years, so the pole star changes over millennia.

concepts.title: Pulsars
concepts.description: Rapidly spinning neutron stars whose beams sweep past Earth like a lighthouse.

concepts.title: Quasars and active galaxies
concepts.description: When a galaxy’s central supermassive black hole feeds, its glowing disk can outshine the whole galaxy: a quasar.

concepts.title: Radio astronomy
concepts.description: Radio telescopes detect long-wavelength radio waves, which pass through dust and can be observed day and night.

concepts.title: Red giants and planetary nebulae
concepts.description: When a Sun-like star’s core runs low on hydrogen, it swells into a red giant, then sheds its outer layers as a glowing planetary nebula.

concepts.title: Redshift
concepts.description: Light from receding galaxies is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths; the farther the galaxy, the bigger the redshift.

concepts.title: Three stellar remnants
concepts.description: White dwarfs are Earth-sized, neutron stars city-sized, and black holes have no surface at all.

concepts.title: Retrograde motion
concepts.description: Planets sometimes appear to move backwards against the stars because Earth overtakes or is overtaken by them.

concepts.title: The four rocky planets
concepts.description: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the small, rocky inner planets.

concepts.title: Ancient scholars knew Earth is round
concepts.description: Greek thinkers had evidence Earth is a sphere, such as its curved shadow on the Moon during lunar eclipses.

concepts.title: The black hole at the center of the Milky Way
concepts.description: Sagittarius A* holds about 4 million times the Sun’s mass; stars orbiting it revealed it.

concepts.title: Saturn's rings are ice
concepts.description: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of water ice, with some rock.

concepts.title: The search for life
concepts.description: Scientists look for biosignatures on Mars and ocean moons and in exoplanet atmospheres, and SETI listens for signals.

concepts.title: Seasons aren't about distance
concepts.description: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter.

concepts.title: Seasons come from Earth's tilt
concepts.description: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun.

concepts.title: Every sky motion has a cause
concepts.description: Daily motion comes from Earth’s spin, yearly changes from Earth’s orbit, and the Moon’s motion and gravity drive phases, eclipses and tides.

concepts.title: Why everything rises in the east
concepts.description: Earth spins west to east, so the Sun, Moon, planets and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

concepts.title: How the solar system formed
concepts.description: About 4.6 billion years ago a spinning cloud of gas and dust collapsed into the Sun and a flat disk that built the planets.

concepts.title: The size of the solar system
concepts.description: The planets span about 30 astronomical units; sunlight takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune.

concepts.title: Solar storms and space weather
concepts.description: The solar wind and eruptions like flares and coronal mass ejections cause auroras and can disrupt technology.

concepts.title: Spectral fingerprints
concepts.description: Each element absorbs and emits its own set of colors, so a spectrum reveals what a star is made of.

concepts.title: Spring and neap tides
concepts.description: When the Sun and Moon line up tides are larger (spring); at right angles they are smaller (neap).

concepts.title: A star's color is its temperature
concepts.description: Blue stars are the hottest; red stars are the coolest.

concepts.title: Where stars are born
concepts.description: Stars form in cold, dense clouds of gas and dust, where gravity pulls clumps together until fusion ignites.

concepts.title: Stars are born, age and die
concepts.description: Stars form in clouds of gas and dust. The Sun will swell into a red giant and end as a white dwarf; massive stars can explode as supernovae.

concepts.title: Navigating by the stars
concepts.description: Before instruments, navigators crossed oceans by memorizing where stars rise and set.

concepts.title: Mass decides a star’s fate
concepts.description: Low-mass stars end as white dwarfs; the most massive leave neutron stars or black holes.

concepts.title: Proof that Earth moves
concepts.description: In 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured stellar parallax, direct evidence that Earth orbits the Sun.

concepts.title: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old
concepts.description: The Sun formed roughly 4.6 billion years ago.

concepts.title: The Sun runs on nuclear fusion
concepts.description: In its core the Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, releasing the energy that becomes sunlight.

concepts.title: The Sun is a star
concepts.description: The Sun is an ordinary star (the closest one to Earth), not a special category of object.

concepts.title: Inside the Sun
concepts.description: Energy made in the Sun’s core travels out through the radiative and convective zones to the photosphere; the corona above is far hotter.

concepts.title: The Sun holds almost all the mass
concepts.description: About 99.8% of the solar system's mass is in the Sun.

concepts.title: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth
concepts.description: Light from the Sun takes roughly eight minutes to cross the distance to Earth, so we always see the Sun slightly in the past.

concepts.title: Sunspots and the solar cycle
concepts.description: Sunspots are cooler, magnetically active regions whose number rises and falls over an ~11-year cycle.

concepts.title: Supernovae and star stuff
concepts.description: Massive stars explode as supernovae, scattering elements forged inside stars, including those in our bodies.

concepts.title: Bigger is better
concepts.description: A telescope’s light-gathering area sets how faint it can see and how fine the detail it can show.

concepts.title: Refractors and reflectors
concepts.description: Refracting telescopes use lenses; reflecting telescopes use mirrors, and all the largest telescopes are reflectors.

concepts.title: The Moon drives the tides
concepts.description: The Moon’s gravity pulls Earth’s oceans into two bulges, so most coasts get two high tides a day.

concepts.title: Titan
concepts.description: Saturn’s largest moon has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane.

concepts.title: Billions of galaxies, 13.8 billion years
concepts.description: The observable universe holds billions of galaxies and is about 13.8 billion years old.

concepts.title: The discovery of Uranus
concepts.description: William Herschel found Uranus in 1781, the first planet discovered with a telescope.

concepts.title: Venus is the hottest planet
concepts.description: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.

concepts.title: Venus: Earth’s twin in size only
concepts.description: Venus is nearly Earth’s size but has crushing pressure, acid clouds and a backwards rotation.

concepts.title: The Voyager probes
concepts.description: Launched in 1977, the twin Voyagers toured the giant planets; Voyager 1 is now in interstellar space.

concepts.title: The James Webb Space Telescope
concepts.description: Launched in 2021, Webb is a huge infrared telescope with a 6.5-meter gold-coated mirror, orbiting the Sun about 1.5 million km from Earth.

concepts.title: White dwarfs
concepts.description: The leftover core of a Sun-like star: about the size of Earth, with much of the Sun’s mass, slowly cooling.

concepts.title: Money as bank deposits
concepts.description: Most money today is bank deposits: records of what banks owe their customers, not physical cash.

concepts.title: Barter and the double coincidence of wants
concepts.description: Barter is trading goods or services directly; it only works when each side wants what the other offers.

concepts.title: Barter in history
concepts.description: No society that ran purely on barter has ever been described; barter tends to appear between acquaintances and when money runs short.

concepts.title: Barter has no common measure
concepts.description: Barter has no single unit for measuring value and makes saving for later hard.

concepts.title: The blockchain ledger
concepts.description: A blockchain is a shared, tamper-evident ledger in which each block of transactions is linked to the one before.

concepts.title: Paying by changing records
concepts.description: A card payment changes banks' records: the payer's balance goes down and the seller's goes up.

concepts.title: Paper money in China
concepts.description: Paper money began in China, from Tang-era flying money to Song-era notes in Sichuan, where heavy iron coins made paper convenient.

concepts.title: What a coin's stamp did
concepts.description: A coin's stamp showed that an authority stood behind a standard weight of metal, so it no longer had to be weighed in every deal.

concepts.title: Cowrie shell money
concepts.description: Cowrie shells served as money in parts of Africa and Asia because they were small, durable and hard to fake.

concepts.title: What a cryptocurrency is
concepts.description: Cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin are digital tokens created and tracked by a network of computers, with no central issuer.

concepts.title: Why crypto prices swing
concepts.description: Bitcoin's price is set by supply and demand; with a nearly fixed supply and no issuer steadying it, the price swings sharply.

concepts.title: Paper money reaches Europe
concepts.description: Marco Polo described Chinese paper money in the 13th century; Europe's first banknotes came from Sweden's Stockholms Banco in 1661.

concepts.title: Fiat money
concepts.description: Fiat money has no value of its own and no commodity backing; a government declares it legal tender.

concepts.title: The gold standard
concepts.description: Under a gold standard, a currency's unit is fixed to a set amount of gold and paper money can be exchanged for it.

concepts.title: Leaving the gold standard
concepts.description: Countries left gold because its supply limited their money; the US ended its last gold link, for foreign governments, in 1971.

concepts.title: The first coins
concepts.description: The first coins were probably made in Lydia, in modern Turkey, around 650 BCE; coinage also arose separately in China.

concepts.title: Why metal made good money
concepts.description: Metal suits money because it is portable, does not perish and is hard to counterfeit.

concepts.title: Six traits of useful money
concepts.description: Useful money is durable, portable, divisible, uniform, limited in supply and acceptable.

concepts.title: The three jobs of money
concepts.description: Money is whatever works as a medium of exchange (a way to pay), a unit of account (a measure of value) and a store of value (a way to save).

concepts.title: Money runs on trust
concepts.description: Money is valuable because people trust that others will accept it; when that trust goes, its value goes too.

concepts.title: Cigarettes as money in a POW camp
concepts.description: In a WWII prisoner-of-war camp described by R. A. Radford in 1945, cigarettes became the currency and did all three jobs of money.

concepts.title: Salt money
concepts.description: In Ethiopia, bars of salt served as money for centuries; salt was useful as well as accepted.

concepts.title: Yap's stone money
concepts.description: On Yap, large stone discs quarried on Palau served as money, changing owners by shared agreement without moving.

concepts.title: Africa across the Equator
concepts.description: The Equator nearly halves Africa, the only continent crossed by the Equator and both tropics, so its climate zones are largely mirrored north and south.

concepts.title: Africa's young population
concepts.description: About 19% of the world's people live in Africa, the youngest continent (median age about 19); Nigeria has the most people.

concepts.title: Africa, the second-largest continent
concepts.description: Africa is the second-largest continent, covering about one-fifth of Earth's land, and flat maps often undersell it.

concepts.title: Africa's great cities
concepts.description: Cairo, Lagos and Kinshasa are among Africa's largest cities; Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other across the Congo River.

concepts.title: Africa's countries
concepts.description: Africa has 54 countries, more than any other continent; Algeria has been the largest since South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011.

concepts.title: The Alpide belt
concepts.description: A second great earthquake belt runs from the Atlantic through the Mediterranean and the Himalayas to Indonesia, along the Alpine-Himalayan ranges.

concepts.title: The Alps, Europe's crumpled water tower
concepts.description: The Alps are fold mountains pushed up by a fragment of the African plate colliding with Eurasia, and their water feeds rivers flowing to four seas.

concepts.title: Air cools as you climb
concepts.description: Near the surface, air cools by about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m you climb, so a tall mountain stacks climates on top of each other.

concepts.title: Climbing through climate zones
concepts.description: Plant zones stack up a mountain like a trip toward the poles, as Humboldt showed on Chimborazo; trees stop at the timberline, and the zones are moving uphill.

concepts.title: The Amazon River
concepts.description: The Amazon rises in the Andes near the Pacific, flows east to the Atlantic, carries about a fifth of Earth's runoff, and drains the world's largest basin.

concepts.title: The Andes
concepts.description: The Andes run along South America's western edge through seven countries, the world's longest continental mountain range.

concepts.title: Claims on Antarctica
concepts.description: Seven countries claim parts of Antarctica, and the claims of Argentina, Chile and the United Kingdom overlap.

concepts.title: The Antarctic ice sheet
concepts.description: Antarctica is a rocky continent under an ice sheet up to 4.8 km thick that holds about 90% of the world's ice and makes it the highest continent.

concepts.title: The Antarctic Treaty
concepts.description: The 1959 Antarctic Treaty freezes territorial claims and keeps Antarctica for peace and science; the 1991 Madrid Protocol bans mining.

concepts.title: Antarctica's extremes
concepts.description: Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent: it holds the lowest measured temperature, gets so little snow it's a desert, and sends katabatic winds pouring off its ice.

concepts.title: Antipodes
concepts.description: A place's antipode is the point directly opposite it through Earth's center: opposite hemisphere, 180° of longitude away, about 12 hours off.

concepts.title: The shrinking Aral Sea
concepts.description: The Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake, shrank after its rivers were diverted in the 1960s to irrigate cotton, bringing harsher climate, toxic dust and collapsed fisheries.

concepts.title: The Arctic: an ocean ringed by land
concepts.description: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by continents, and sea ice floating on it covers the North Pole.

concepts.title: Arctic sea ice
concepts.description: Arctic sea ice grows to a maximum in March and shrinks to a minimum in September; the September minimum is shrinking about 12% per decade, and losing reflective ice speeds warming.

concepts.title: Most people on Earth live in Asia
concepts.description: About three-fifths of humanity lives in Asia, crowded into South Asia, eastern China and the Pacific coasts and islands.

concepts.title: Asia's regions and empty spaces
concepts.description: Asia, the largest continent, divides into East, South, Southeast, Central, West and North Asia, and much of its interior is thinly peopled.

concepts.title: How atolls form
concepts.description: A reef fringing a volcanic island keeps growing upward as the island sinks; when the island disappears, a ring of reef around a lagoon remains, as Darwin proposed and drilling confirmed.

concepts.title: Australians live on the coast
concepts.description: Most Australians live near the coast, especially the fertile east coast, beyond which the Great Dividing Range separates the cities from the Outback.

concepts.title: Australia: a dry continent-country
concepts.description: Australia is the smallest continent and one of the largest countries; except for Antarctica it's the driest continent, with a vast arid interior called the Outback.

concepts.title: What a biome is
concepts.description: A biome is a large area defined by its vegetation, soil, climate and wildlife; the five major types are forest, grassland, desert, tundra and aquatic.

concepts.title: How borders are drawn
concepts.description: Some borders follow natural features like mountains and rivers; others are straight lines such as the 49th parallel; borders drawn without regard to local communities often cause conflict.

concepts.title: The taiga (boreal forest)
concepts.description: The taiga is the largest land biome: a belt of water-saving, snow-shedding conifers across the far north.

concepts.title: Cardinal directions
concepts.description: North, east, south and west; Earth spins toward the east, so the Sun rises roughly in the east.

concepts.title: The Caribbean islands
concepts.description: The West Indies curve in a long crescent: the big Greater Antilles, led by Cuba, and the smaller Lesser Antilles.

concepts.title: The Central American isthmus
concepts.description: Central America is a narrow isthmus of seven countries linking North and South America, with a wetter Caribbean coast.

concepts.title: Climate normals
concepts.description: Climate is usually summarized as 30-year averages; NOAA updates its US normals every 10 years.

concepts.title: Climate shapes biomes
concepts.description: Temperature and precipitation decide which biome grows where, so similar climates grow similar-looking biomes, even from unrelated plants.

concepts.title: Where climate zones occur
concepts.description: Tropical climates sit near the Equator, big hot deserts about 15 to 30 degrees out, continental climates inside big landmasses, polar climates near the poles.

concepts.title: Mountains from colliding plates
concepts.description: When India hit Eurasia, neither plate could sink, so the crust crumpled upward into the still-rising Himalayas.

concepts.title: The Congo rainforest
concepts.description: The Congo Basin holds the world's second-largest rainforest; bonobos live only south of the Congo River.

concepts.title: The Congo River
concepts.description: The Congo crosses the Equator twice, so part of its basin is always in a rainy season and it flows steadily; only the Amazon carries more water.

concepts.title: Continents by size
concepts.description: Asia is the largest continent and Australia the smallest.

concepts.title: The Continental Divide
concepts.description: A ridge along the crests of the Rockies and the Andes separates rivers that flow to the Pacific from those that flow to the Atlantic side.

concepts.title: Continental drift and Pangaea
concepts.description: Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents were once joined in Pangaea; the idea was accepted once plate tectonics explained the motion.

concepts.title: Coordinates and 0°, 0°
concepts.description: A latitude and a longitude together fix one spot; the point 0°, 0° lies in open ocean in the Gulf of Guinea.

concepts.title: Corals are animals
concepts.description: Corals are animals: tiny polyps that build limestone skeletons and live in partnership with food-making algae.

concepts.title: Coral bleaching
concepts.description: Corals stressed by warm water expel the algae that feed and color them, turning white; prolonged bleaching kills them, and climate change is the reef's greatest threat.

concepts.title: The Coriolis effect
concepts.description: Earth's rotation deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.

concepts.title: Hurricane, typhoon or cyclone
concepts.description: The same storm is called a hurricane, typhoon or cyclone depending on the ocean where it forms.

concepts.title: The International Date Line
concepts.description: The date line roughly follows the 180° meridian; crossing it westward moves the calendar a day ahead.

concepts.title: The Dead Sea
concepts.description: The Dead Sea lies more than 400 m below sea level, Earth's lowest land, and is so salty that swimmers float.

concepts.title: Ocean dead zones
concepts.description: Nutrient runoff from farms and cities feeds algae; when they die and decompose they use up oxygen, creating dead zones such as the one off the Mississippi every summer.

concepts.title: Deciduous forests and autumn
concepts.description: Winter makes water scarce, so deciduous trees shed their leaves; autumn yellows appear when chlorophyll breaks down and reveals hidden pigments.

concepts.title: Deserts are defined by dryness
concepts.description: A desert is defined by very little precipitation, not by heat, so icy Antarctica is the largest desert and the Sahara the largest hot one.

concepts.title: How deserts form
concepts.description: Deserts form under belts of dry sinking air around 30° to 35° N and S, and in the rain shadows of mountains.

concepts.title: Evidence the continents were joined
concepts.description: Matching coastlines, matching rock layers and fossils like Mesosaurus show Africa and South America were once joined.

concepts.title: Earth's metal core
concepts.description: The core is iron and nickel: a liquid outer core that makes the magnetic field and a solid inner core, revealed by earthquake waves.

concepts.title: Crust and mantle
concepts.description: Earth's thin rocky crust sits on the mantle, a thick layer of solid rock that flows very slowly over long periods.

concepts.title: Earth's connected systems
concepts.description: Earth works as connected systems of rock, water, air, life and ice (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere, cryosphere) that constantly interact.

concepts.title: What causes earthquakes
concepts.description: Stuck plate edges build up force until rock suddenly slips along a fault, sending out seismic waves from the hypocenter.

concepts.title: Earthquake magnitude
concepts.description: Each whole step in magnitude means about 32 times more energy; the largest recorded earthquake was magnitude 9.5.

concepts.title: Elevation and contour lines
concepts.description: Heights are measured above sea level, and contour lines join points of equal elevation; close lines mean steep ground.

concepts.title: Equal-area maps
concepts.description: Equal-area projections show the true relative sizes of places but distort their shapes.

concepts.title: The Equator
concepts.description: The Equator is 0° latitude, halfway between the poles, splitting Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

concepts.title: Landforms carved by erosion
concepts.description: Waves carve caves, arches and sea stacks; wind shapes rock and dunes; glaciers widen valleys.

concepts.title: Europe, a peninsula of Eurasia
concepts.description: Europe is the western peninsula of Eurasia, bounded by the Urals and three bodies of water, and itself a peninsula of peninsulas.

concepts.title: Europe's four physical regions
concepts.description: From north to south Europe falls into the Western Uplands, the North European Plain, the Central Uplands and the Alpine Mountains.

concepts.title: The Rhine and the Danube
concepts.description: The Rhine runs from the Alps to the North Sea and the Danube from the Black Forest to the Black Sea; a canal now links them.

concepts.title: Where water vapor comes from
concepts.description: Most water vapor evaporates from oceans and other open water, plants add more by transpiration, and a molecule stays aloft only about 10 days.

concepts.title: Everest's sea-floor summit
concepts.description: The rock at Everest's summit is limestone from an ancient sea floor, full of marine fossils, lifted by the collision.

concepts.title: How much land feeds us
concepts.description: Almost half of the world's habitable land is farmed, and more than three-quarters of that farmland goes to livestock, which supply under a fifth of calories.

concepts.title: Five named oceans, one world ocean
concepts.description: The Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic are named regions of one connected global ocean; the Southern is the newest named.

concepts.title: Forced displacement
concepts.description: At the end of 2024, 123.2 million people were forcibly displaced; most stayed inside their own countries, and most refugees are hosted by neighbouring countries.

concepts.title: How little water is fresh
concepts.description: Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is ice or groundwater; lakes and rivers hold a tiny fraction.

concepts.title: Scarce fresh water
concepts.description: Almost all of Earth's water is salty ocean, and most fresh water is locked in ice, so usable fresh water is a scarce resource.

concepts.title: Lakes dug by ice
concepts.description: Massive glaciers scoured and deepened old valleys in the middle of North America, making the basins the Great Lakes now fill.

concepts.title: How glaciers form and flow
concepts.description: Glaciers form where snow survives year after year and is squeezed into ice; they flow slowly downhill under their own weight.

concepts.title: Earth is warming
concepts.description: Burning fossil fuels has raised carbon dioxide by more than 50%, and Earth has warmed about 1°C, mostly because of human activity.

concepts.title: How GPS finds you
concepts.description: A receiver turns signal travel times into distances and needs four satellites: three for position, one to fix its clock.

concepts.title: The GPS constellation
concepts.description: At least 24 GPS satellites with precise clocks broadcast one-way signals of their position and time.

concepts.title: How the Grand Canyon was carved
concepts.description: The land was lifted into the Colorado Plateau, then the Colorado River cut down through it over the last 5 to 6 million years.

concepts.title: The canyon's rock record
concepts.description: The Grand Canyon exposes layers of rock with the oldest, nearly 2 billion years old, at the bottom and younger layers above.

concepts.title: Grasslands
concepts.description: Grasslands grow between forest and desert on the rainfall scale; fire, drought and grazing keep them open, and grass regrows from its base.

concepts.title: The Great Barrier Reef
concepts.description: The world's largest coral reef system stretches more than 2,000 km off northeastern Australia, built by colonies of tiny animals called polyps.

concepts.title: The Great Lakes
concepts.description: Five lakes, Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario, hold about a fifth of the world's surface fresh water and drain east to the Atlantic.

concepts.title: The Great Plains
concepts.description: East of the Rockies, the Great Plains form a dry, windy grassland that slopes gently down toward the east.

concepts.title: The Great Rift Valley
concepts.description: East Africa is being pulled apart as the Somali plate separates from the Nubian plate; the Red Sea is a rift the sea already flooded.

concepts.title: The green Sahara
concepts.description: About 11,000 years ago a wobble in Earth's axis pushed monsoon rains north and the Sahara held lakes, rivers and grasslands before drying out.

concepts.title: The greenhouse effect
concepts.description: Greenhouse gases trap some of the heat Earth gives off; without them Earth would average about -18°C.

concepts.title: Groundwater and aquifers
concepts.description: Groundwater fills pores and cracks in rock and soil, like water in a sponge; usable amounts sit in aquifers reached by wells.

concepts.title: Persian Gulf oil
concepts.description: The Persian Gulf countries hold about half the world's proved crude oil reserves, formed from ancient marine life.

concepts.title: Water scarcity and desalination
concepts.description: The Middle East and North Africa have very little fresh water, so Gulf countries desalinate seawater using their oil and gas.

concepts.title: The Hadley cell
concepts.description: A loop of air: rising and raining at the Equator, sinking and drying near 30 degrees, returning as the trade winds.

concepts.title: How the Himalayas rose
concepts.description: India collided with Asia 40 to 50 million years ago; the crust crumpled upward, lifting ancient seafloor to Everest's summit, and it is still rising.

concepts.title: The abode of snow
concepts.description: The Himalayas' snow and glaciers feed great rivers, including the Indus, the Brahmaputra and the Ganges.

concepts.title: Hokulea's 1976 voyage
concepts.description: In 1976 the canoe Hokulea sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti with no instruments, showing that Polynesians could have settled the Pacific by deliberate voyages.

concepts.title: Hotspots
concepts.description: Some volcanoes, like Hawaii's, form over a stationary hotspot in the mantle, far from plate boundaries.

concepts.title: Hurricane season
concepts.description: Hurricanes feed on warm tropical water, so the Atlantic season runs June to November and peaks in September, when the ocean is warmest.

concepts.title: Ice-age sea level
concepts.description: In the last ice age so much water was frozen on land that sea level fell by about 120 m, uncovering the Beringia land bridge between Asia and North America.

concepts.title: Earth's two ice sheets
concepts.description: Only Greenland and Antarctica have ice sheets today; together they hold over 68% of Earth's fresh water, and melting Antarctica would raise the sea about 58 m.

concepts.title: Iceland's rift
concepts.description: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, and over a hotspot.

concepts.title: International migrants
concepts.description: About 304 million people, 3.7% of the world or 1 in 27, were international migrants in 2024; the United States hosts the most.

concepts.title: Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak
concepts.description: Kilimanjaro, a volcano about 3° south of the Equator, rises 5,895 m and is the highest point in Africa.

concepts.title: The Köppen climate groups
concepts.description: Köppen's system, built on vegetation zones, sorts climates into five groups: tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar.

concepts.title: How lakes form
concepts.description: Lakes fill inland basins; glaciers dug most of them, and rifts in the crust dug others, like Baikal, the deepest and oldest lake.

concepts.title: Plateaus, valleys and deltas
concepts.description: Three common landforms: raised flat plateaus, valleys carved by rivers and glaciers, and deltas built at river mouths.

concepts.title: Language families
concepts.description: A language family is a group of languages descended from one ancestor; Indo-European, from Proto-Indo-European, spans most of Europe and much of South and Southwest Asia.

concepts.title: Latitude
concepts.description: Latitude measures distance north or south of the Equator, from 0° to 90°, along parallel lines.

concepts.title: Longitude and the prime meridian
concepts.description: Longitude measures distance east or west of the prime meridian through Greenwich, chosen in 1884, from 0° to 180°.

concepts.title: Longshore drift
concepts.description: Waves usually meet the beach at an angle, setting up a current parallel to shore that carries sand along the coast.

concepts.title: How a compass works
concepts.description: A compass needle is a magnet that lines up with Earth's magnetic field.

concepts.title: Magnetic north vs true north
concepts.description: The North Magnetic Pole is not the Geographic North Pole and drifts; the angle between them is magnetic declination.

concepts.title: The major world religions
concepts.description: In 2020 Christians were about 29% of the world, Muslims about 26%, the unaffiliated about 24%, Hindus about 15% and Buddhists about 4%; Muslims grew fastest.

concepts.title: Every flat map distorts
concepts.description: A round Earth can't be flattened without distortion, so every flat map sacrifices some accuracy that a globe keeps.

concepts.title: The Mediterranean climate
concepts.description: Hot, dry summers and cool, wet winters, found around the Mediterranean and at about 30 to 45 degrees latitude on western coasts.

concepts.title: The Mediterranean, a sea that connected peoples
concepts.description: The Mediterranean sits between Europe, Africa and Asia, and ancient seafarers settled all around it.

concepts.title: Megacities and the largest cities
concepts.description: A megacity has 10 million or more people; there were 33 in 2025. By the UN's 2025 count, Jakarta, Dhaka and Tokyo are the largest, and rankings depend on how a city is measured.

concepts.title: The Mercator projection
concepts.description: Mercator's 1569 map keeps compass bearings straight for navigation but inflates areas far from the Equator.

concepts.title: The Tigris, the Euphrates and Mesopotamia
concepts.description: Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates, is fertile but dry, so farming there relied on irrigation from the rivers.

concepts.title: The Mexican Plateau
concepts.description: Mexico's heartland is a high plateau between two Sierra Madre ranges, its largest and most densely populated region.

concepts.title: Volcanoes of Mexico and Central America
concepts.description: Mexico and Central America sit where several plates meet, so volcanoes like Parícutin and Citlaltépetl are common.

concepts.title: The Middle East
concepts.description: A loosely defined region centered on Southwest Asia, often including Egypt; much of it is desert, including the Rub' al Khali sand sea.

concepts.title: Why people migrate
concepts.description: People migrate because of push factors (war, food shortages, floods) and pull factors (jobs, better climate, food supply), within a country or across borders.

concepts.title: The Mississippi River
concepts.description: The Mississippi runs from a wadeable stream at Lake Itasca to a vast delta on the Gulf of Mexico.

concepts.title: The Mississippi's watershed
concepts.description: The Mississippi and its tributaries drain all or part of 31 states and two Canadian provinces, about 40% of the continental US.

concepts.title: Monsoons
concepts.description: Seasonal wind reversals driven by land heating faster than ocean; South Asia's summer monsoon brings most of India's rain.

concepts.title: The Nile's yearly flood
concepts.description: Each summer the Nile's flood spread dark, fertile silt over Egypt's fields, giving the land its name, Kemet, until the Aswan High Dam ended it in 1970.

concepts.title: The Nile flood and Egyptian farming
concepts.description: The Nile's annual flood left fertile silt that made farming possible in a desert, until the Aswan High Dam ended the flood in 1970.

concepts.title: The Nile and its branches
concepts.description: The Nile flows north to the Mediterranean; the White and Blue Niles meet at Khartoum, and the Blue Nile brings most of the water and silt.

concepts.title: North America's reach
concepts.description: North America stretches from near the North Pole almost to the Equator, and takes in Canada, the US, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and Greenland.

concepts.title: North America's shape
concepts.description: North America has an ancient rock core (the Canadian Shield), old worn mountains in the east, younger taller mountains in the west, and flat plains between.

concepts.title: New Zealand's volcanoes and geysers
concepts.description: In the North Island the Pacific Plate slides under the Australian Plate; melting rock feeds volcanoes like Ruapehu and heats water for the geysers and hot springs of Rotorua and Taupo.

concepts.title: New Zealand's plate boundary
concepts.description: New Zealand straddles the Australian and Pacific plates; in the South Island they meet along the Alpine Fault, pushing up the Southern Alps.

concepts.title: The deep-ocean conveyor belt
concepts.description: Deep currents are driven by density: cold, salty water sinks, keeping a slow global loop moving that takes about 1,000 years.

concepts.title: How deep the ocean goes
concepts.description: The ocean averages about 3,700 m deep, and its deepest point, Challenger Deep, is about 11 km down: deeper than Everest is tall.

concepts.title: Oceans by size
concepts.description: The Pacific is the largest ocean, bigger than all land combined; the Arctic is the smallest.

concepts.title: High islands and low islands
concepts.description: Pacific islands are either high volcanic islands built by eruptions or low coral islands, often atolls ringing a lagoon.

concepts.title: The Pan-American Highway
concepts.description: A road network runs from Alaska to the tip of Argentina, broken only by the Darién Gap between Panama and Colombia.

concepts.title: Permafrost
concepts.description: Permafrost is ground frozen for at least two years; only a thin top layer thaws in summer, so meltwater is trapped and the tundra turns soggy.

concepts.title: Plate boundaries
concepts.description: Plates pull apart at divergent boundaries, push together at convergent ones and slide past each other at transform boundaries.

concepts.title: The polar circles
concepts.description: The Arctic and Antarctic Circles, at about 66.5°, mark where the Sun stays up or down for a full day at least once a year.

concepts.title: Polar opposites
concepts.description: The Arctic is ocean ringed by land and Antarctica land ringed by ocean; the high, ocean-less South Pole is far colder, and the two poles take turns with six months of sunlight.

concepts.title: Where people live
concepts.description: People are spread unevenly: about 60% live in the Asia-Pacific region, India is the most populous country, and about 87% live north of the Equator.

concepts.title: Air pressure makes wind
concepts.description: Air flows from high pressure to low pressure; uneven heating by the Sun creates the pressure differences.

concepts.title: Rain shadows
concepts.description: Mountains force moist air up, so the windward side gets rain and the leeward side is left dry: a rain shadow.

concepts.title: Why rainforests teem with life
concepts.description: Year-round sunlight and moisture let rainforests hold more than half of the world's species on a small slice of the surface.

concepts.title: Reefs: crowded cities of the sea
concepts.description: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean but hold nearly a quarter of its species, in clear, warm, sunlit tropical water.

concepts.title: Coral bleaching
concepts.description: Water that is too warm makes corals expel their algae and turn white; they can recover if the heat eases, or die if it lasts.

concepts.title: Where religions are practiced
concepts.description: Religions are unevenly spread: most Muslims, nearly all Hindus and nearly all Buddhists live in the Asia-Pacific region, and sub-Saharan Africa now has the most Christians.

concepts.title: The resource curse
concepts.description: Countries rich in natural resources often grow more slowly than resource-poor ones, partly through conflict over resources; Botswana is a noted exception.

concepts.title: Where resources are found
concepts.description: Natural resources are unevenly spread: Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves and the Democratic Republic of the Congo mines most of the world's cobalt.

concepts.title: The rift and human origins
concepts.description: The Rift Valley yields key early human fossils such as Lucy, and its datable volcanic ash layers let scientists date them.

concepts.title: The Ring of Fire
concepts.description: A belt of plate boundaries around the Pacific holds about 75% of Earth's volcanoes and 90% of its earthquakes.

concepts.title: River valleys and the first civilizations
concepts.description: Many of the earliest civilizations grew up in river valleys, where water and fertile soil made farming and irrigation possible.

concepts.title: The longest rivers
concepts.description: The Nile, about 6,650 km, is usually ranked longest, but the Amazon (at least 6,400 km) disputes it because experts disagree on where rivers start and end.

concepts.title: The rock cycle
concepts.description: Any type of rock can become any other; limestone becomes marble and granite becomes gneiss under heat and pressure.

concepts.title: The three kinds of rock
concepts.description: Igneous rock cools from molten rock, sedimentary rock forms from pressed layers, metamorphic rock is changed by heat and pressure.

concepts.title: The Rocky Mountains
concepts.description: The Rockies run some 4,800 km from northern Canada to New Mexico, the best-known range of the western mountains.

concepts.title: Russia and Siberia
concepts.description: Russia is by far the largest country; most Russians live in its European part, while Siberia covers most of the land.

concepts.title: Russia's eleven time zones
concepts.description: Russia is so wide that it spans 11 time zones, and its longest railway crosses eight of them.

concepts.title: The Sahara, largest hot desert
concepts.description: A desert is defined by low precipitation; the Sahara is the largest hot desert (Antarctica is the largest overall), and most of it is rock and gravel, not sand.

concepts.title: Why some lakes are salty
concepts.description: Rivers carry dissolved salt from rocks; a lake with no outlet loses water only by evaporation, so its salt builds up, as in the Dead Sea.

concepts.title: Savannas
concepts.description: A savanna is a hot, seasonally dry grassland with scattered trees; the largest are in Africa, and fire keeps the trees in check.

concepts.title: Seas and oceans
concepts.description: Seas are smaller parts of the ocean, usually partly enclosed by land; the Sargasso Sea is the one exception, bounded only by currents.

concepts.title: The seven continents
concepts.description: Earth's land is commonly divided into seven continents; Antarctica is the only one with no permanent population.

concepts.title: Africa's shrinking mountain ice
concepts.description: Glaciers near the Equator on Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya are retreating; Kilimanjaro has lost more than 85% of its summit ice since 1912.

concepts.title: South America's countries
concepts.description: South America has 12 independent countries plus French Guiana; Brazil covers about half the continent, and Ecuador is named after the Equator.

concepts.title: South America's shape
concepts.description: South America is broad in the north and tapers south, with the Andes in the west, the Amazon basin in the north, plains in the east and center, and Patagonia in the south.

concepts.title: South Asia's landscapes and people
concepts.description: The Indian subcontinent has three great units, the Himalayas, the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the Deccan plateau, and India is now the most populous country.

concepts.title: How many countries?
concepts.description: The UN has 193 member states and 2 observer states, but lists of countries differ because places like Kosovo and Taiwan are not UN members.

concepts.title: The crops that feed the world
concepts.description: Just 15 crops give 90% of the world's food energy, and rice, maize and wheat give two-thirds of that; rice, mostly grown in Asia-Pacific, feeds almost half of humanity.

concepts.title: Subduction makes volcanoes
concepts.description: Where one plate is pushed beneath another, the sinking rock helps make magma that rises and erupts.

concepts.title: The Suez Canal
concepts.description: The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean and Red Seas without locks, separates Africa from Asia and lets ships skip sailing around Africa.

concepts.title: Sun angle and heating
concepts.description: Sunlight arrives more directly near the Equator and spreads over larger areas toward the poles, so the tropics get the most energy; tilt, not distance, drives the seasons.

concepts.title: Surface currents carry heat
concepts.description: Winds drive surface currents, which carry warm water from the Equator toward the poles; the Gulf Stream warms northwestern Europe.

concepts.title: Tectonic plates
concepts.description: Earth's outer shell is broken into rocky plates that carry continents and oceans and move a few centimeters a year.

concepts.title: Thunderstorms and lightning
concepts.description: Thunderstorms need moisture, unstable air and lift; lightning heats air so fast it expands into thunder.

concepts.title: Time zones
concepts.description: Because Earth turns 15° an hour, the world uses 24 standard time zones counted from Greenwich, with borders bent to follow countries.

concepts.title: Tornadoes
concepts.description: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air from a thunderstorm to the ground; the US has the most.

concepts.title: The trade winds
concepts.description: Steady easterly winds near the Equator, bent by the Coriolis effect, that once carried sailing ships to the Americas.

concepts.title: How tropical cyclones work
concepts.description: Tropical cyclones feed on warm ocean water, spin because of the Coriolis effect, and weaken over land.

concepts.title: Tropical rainforests
concepts.description: Tropical rainforests grow in the tropics, warm and wet all year, and are built in four layers from sunny emergents to the dark forest floor.

concepts.title: The tropics
concepts.description: The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, at about 23.5° N and S because of Earth's tilt, bound the only zone where the Sun is ever directly overhead.

concepts.title: How tsunamis travel
concepts.description: Tsunamis race across deep ocean as low waves, then slow and grow tall in shallow water; the sea may pull back first.

concepts.title: How tsunamis form
concepts.description: Undersea earthquakes lift or drop the seafloor, shoving the whole water column and launching a tsunami.

concepts.title: The tundra
concepts.description: The tundra is cold, treeless land of low plants, found beyond the Arctic Circle and high on mountains.

concepts.title: Uluru and the Anangu
concepts.description: Uluru is sacred to its Aboriginal Traditional Owners, the Anangu; the park was handed back in 1985 and the climb closed in 2019.

concepts.title: Uluru, the rock
concepts.description: Uluru rises 348 m from the Outback plain, is only the tip of a much bigger buried slab, and gets its red color from rusting iron.

concepts.title: Why cities grow
concepts.description: Cities grow as people move in from the countryside for jobs and opportunities; they began to boom with industrialization in the 18th century.

concepts.title: How volcanoes form
concepts.description: Magma rises because it is lighter than solid rock and erupts as lava, mostly near plate boundaries where sinking plates melt.

concepts.title: The water cycle
concepts.description: Water circulates between ocean, air and land, lifted by the Sun's energy and pulled back by gravity, while the total amount stays about the same.

concepts.title: Earth is mostly water
concepts.description: About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water, so ocean, not land, dominates the planet.

concepts.title: Watersheds and river flow
concepts.description: A watershed is all the land draining to one outlet; the Amazon's is the world's largest, and it carries about a fifth of the water running off Earth's surface.

concepts.title: Waves wear coasts away
concepts.description: Wind-made waves carry energy to the coast, carving arches that collapse into sea stacks, which erode away in turn.

concepts.title: Polynesian wayfinding
concepts.description: Polynesian navigators found their way without instruments by the rising and setting points of stars, ocean swells, homing seabirds and clouds over islands.

concepts.title: Weather vs climate
concepts.description: Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere; climate is the long-term average weather of a place.

concepts.title: Weathering and erosion
