The Senate ended the empire by a vote
Life in Italy went on much as before

questions.explanation: For many people little changed at once, so 476 CE is more a marker than a sudden end.

questions.prompt: From Level 44: the name Augustulus means “little Augustus.” Who was the first Augustus?
questions.explanation: In 27 BCE the Senate gave Octavian the name Augustus.

levels.title: Why Did Rome Fall?
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the main explanations for the fall of the Western Empire.
levels.summary: Invasions, civil wars and the loss of Africa broke the West. Gibbon blamed Christianity and lost virtue; others see a transformation.

cards.headline: Historians have given many answers to why the West fell. Here are the big ones.
cards.body: The West fell in 476 CE. Fine. But why? Historians have proposed many answers, and one twist: maybe “fall” is the wrong word.

cards.headline: Outside and inside
cards.body: Start with the squeeze. From outside, pressure from Germanic peoples and the Huns stretched the western army beyond its limits. From inside, repeated civil wars between Roman generals weakened the West further. Then came the money. When the Vandals captured Carthage in 439 CE, the West lost its richest tax base and a major grain supply. Enemies at the door, fights in the house, and an empty pantry.

cards.headline: Fall or transformation?
cards.body: The classic answer came from Edward Gibbon, the historian who called the age of the Five Good Emperors the happiest (Level 60). His The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire blamed, in part, the rise of Christianity and a loss of civic virtue. Some historians today tell it differently: not a sudden collapse, but a transformation into the kingdoms of medieval Europe. Less a house falling down, more a house slowly remodeled by new owners.

cards.fact: The richer half survived.
cards.context: The East was richer and more populous than the West, which helps explain why it outlived the West by nearly a thousand years (you’ll meet it next level). Two halves of one empire, and the one with more money and more people was the one still standing.

cards.headline: The fall: debated
learned: Invasions stretched the western army
Civil wars weakened the West
Losing Africa cost taxes and grain
Some see transformation, not collapse

questions.prompt: What did the West lose when the Vandals took Carthage in 439 CE?

options.label: Its only fleet of warships
options.rationale: The loss was money and food.

options.label: Its last Roman legion
options.rationale: The loss was money and food.

questions.explanation: Africa was the West’s richest tax base and a major grain supply.

questions.prompt: Why do some historians prefer “transformation” to “fall”?

options.label: The West was never actually invaded
The West changed gradually into new kingdoms
Rome was rebuilt better within ten years
The East peacefully absorbed the whole West

questions.explanation: They see Roman ways blending into the kingdoms of medieval Europe rather than a sudden collapse.

questions.prompt: From Level 60: which historian, author of The Decline and Fall, praised the Five Good Emperors?

options.label: Tacitus
options.rationale: He lived in the Roman era.

options.label: Livy
options.rationale: He lived in the Roman era.

questions.explanation: Edward Gibbon called the age of the Five Good Emperors the happiest, then wrote of Rome’s decline.

levels.title: The Empire That Didn't Fall
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Eastern Roman Empire lasted until 1453.
levels.summary: The Greek-speaking East called itself Roman. Justinian won back Italy and built Hagia Sophia; Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

cards.headline: The Roman Empire lasted until 1453, if you count the East.
cards.body: The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, outlived the West by nearly a thousand years. So when did Rome really end? Depends which half you ask.

cards.headline: Romans in the East
cards.body: Historians call the Eastern Roman Empire the Byzantine Empire. That’s our label, not theirs: its people called themselves Romans. Their capital was Constantinople, which Constantine dedicated in 330 CE. Over time, though, Greek replaced Latin as the language of its government. So picture it: Romans, running the Roman Empire, in Greek.

cards.headline: Justinian’s ambition
cards.body: In the 6th century CE, the emperor Justinian reconquered Italy and North Africa, for a time. The old West was briefly Roman again. He also had Roman law collected into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the “body of civil law.” And he built the great church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, finished in 537 CE. Land, law and a landmark: not a bad record for a “fallen” empire.

cards.fact: Constantinople fell in 1453 CE.
cards.context: Sultan Mehmed II led the Ottoman capture of the city, more than a thousand years after Constantine dedicated it in 330 CE. That’s the last page of Roman history, if you count the East. The city itself carried on under a new name: today it’s Istanbul.

cards.headline: The East: endured
learned: The Byzantines called themselves Romans
Greek became the language of government
Justinian reconquered Italy for a time
Constantinople fell in 1453 CE

questions.prompt: What did the people of the “Byzantine” Empire call themselves?

options.label: Greeks
options.rationale: They spoke Greek, but not that.

questions.explanation: Its people called themselves Romans; “Byzantine” is a later historians’ label.

questions.prompt: Which language came to run the eastern empire’s government?
questions.explanation: Over time Greek replaced Latin as the language of government in the East.

questions.prompt: From Level 77: what did Justinian have Roman law collected into?
questions.explanation: Justinian’s Corpus Juris Civilis became the base of the world’s civil law systems.

levels.title: Integration: Rome in Our Laws and Governments
levels.objective: After this level you can connect Roman institutions to modern republics and legal systems.
levels.summary: Senates, capitols, vetoes and balanced constitutions come from Rome, and Justinian’s code underlies civil law across much of the world.

cards.headline: Every time a president vetoes a bill, they are speaking Latin.
cards.body: Veto is Latin for “I forbid.” And that’s just one of the things Rome left inside modern governments. Let’s count them.

cards.headline: Names we kept
cards.body: Start with the names. Rome’s Senate began as a council of elders advising the king, and the United States Senate takes its name from it. The US Capitol is named after Rome’s Capitoline Hill, home of its greatest temple, dedicated to Jupiter, king of the gods. And veto? A Roman tribune could block other magistrates by declaring “Veto.” Today the word still means the power to block laws, as when a US president vetoes a bill. Same word, same job.

cards.headline: Ideas we kept
cards.body: Names are easy to borrow. Ideas matter more. The Greek historian Polybius praised Rome’s government as a mix: consuls like monarchs, a Senate of aristocrats, and assemblies for the people, each checking the others. The framers of the US Constitution studied the Roman Republic and its balance between different parts of government. And Justinian’s code shaped the civil law systems of continental Europe, Latin America and many other countries. Rome’s rules still run courtrooms Rome never saw.

cards.headline: The laws: traced
learned: The US Senate is named for Rome’s
The Capitol recalls the Capitoline Hill
Veto still means “I forbid”
Civil law grew from Justinian’s code

questions.prompt: What does a US president do by vetoing a bill?

options.label: Sends it to the Senate floor
Asks the courts to review it

questions.explanation: The word veto is still used for the power to block laws, just as a tribune once blocked a magistrate.

questions.prompt: What did the US framers take from the Roman Republic?

options.label: The Twelve Tables word for word
Rule by a dictator for life
A balance between parts of government

questions.explanation: They studied the Republic’s balance between offices, the mix Polybius had praised.

questions.prompt: From Level 7: the US Capitol is named for the hill of Rome’s greatest temple. Whom did that temple honor?

options.label: Mars, the god of war
options.rationale: It honored the king of the gods.

options.label: Vesta, the goddess of the hearth
Janus, the god of doors
options.rationale: It honored the king of the gods.

questions.explanation: The Capitoline temple was dedicated to Jupiter, with Juno and Minerva.

levels.title: Integration: Rome in Our Words, Calendars and Cities
levels.objective: After this level you can trace Rome's legacy in languages, calendars, architecture and city planning.
levels.summary: Roman towns became London and Paris, Roman columns became capitols and banks, and July and August still honor Caesar and Augustus.

cards.headline: You can see Rome in a city map, a bank front and a calendar.
cards.body: The empire is long gone. Its fingerprints aren’t. Let’s go looking for them.

cards.headline: Cities and buildings
cards.body: Many European cities grew from Roman towns or forts, including London, Paris, Cologne and Vienna. Many Roman towns were laid out on a grid, with two main streets crossing at right angles. Much later, neoclassical architecture copied Roman columns, domes and temple fronts in buildings across Europe and the Americas. Next time you pass a bank with columns out front, you’re looking at a Roman idea wearing a suit.

cards.headline: Words and time
cards.body: Everyday spoken Latin kept changing until it became Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian. English isn’t one of those Romance languages, but a large share of its vocabulary comes from Latin, much of it through French. Now check a calendar. July is named for Julius Caesar, and August for Augustus. Rome’s two most famous names, still sitting side by side every year.

cards.fact: “E pluribus unum”: out of many, one.
cards.context: Latin mottoes still appear on seals and coins. This one sits on the Great Seal of the United States: a modern country describing itself in Rome’s language.

cards.headline: The legacy: traced
learned: Many European cities grew from Roman towns
Roman towns used grids
Neoclassical builders copied Rome
Latin lives on in words and mottoes

questions.prompt: Which of these cities grew from a Roman town?
questions.explanation: London was founded by the Romans; Paris, Cologne and Vienna also grew from Roman towns or forts.

questions.prompt: Why do so many capitols and banks have columns and domes?

options.label: They were built by Roman engineers

questions.explanation: Neoclassical architecture copied Roman columns, domes and temple fronts to borrow Rome’s prestige.

questions.prompt: From Level 48: which month honors Rome’s first emperor?
questions.explanation: Sextilis was renamed Augustus, our August, in 8 BCE.

levels.title: Integration: How We Know About Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how historians use texts, inscriptions, coins and archaeology to study Rome.
levels.summary: Ancient writers had biases, so historians test them against inscriptions, coins, letters and the archaeology of places like Pompeii.

cards.headline: A history of Rome is a detective story built from four kinds of clues.
cards.body: Texts, inscriptions, coins and the ground itself. Each clue tells part of the truth. None tells all of it.

cards.headline: Texts and their biases
cards.body: The obvious clue is the written word. Much of Roman history comes from ancient writers such as Livy, Tacitus and Suetonius. But each had his own sources, purposes and biases. Most accounts of Caligula come from later writers hostile to him, so historians treat the wildest stories with caution. And Rome’s founding stories were written down centuries after the events. Picture a witness who wasn’t there, and one who didn’t like the suspect.

cards.headline: Stone, metal and earth
cards.body: So historians check the writers against other clues. Huge numbers of Latin inscriptions carved in stone record laws, careers, dedications and epitaphs. Coins help date events and show how emperors wanted to be seen: each one a tiny press release in your pocket. Archaeology reveals the ordinary lives writers ignored, from houses and graves to rubbish heaps. Yes, Roman trash counts as evidence.

cards.fact: Ordinary Romans speak through the ground.
cards.context: Pompeii gives historians a rare snapshot of ordinary Roman town life. At Vindolanda, a fort near Hadrian’s Wall, archaeologists found more than a thousand wooden writing tablets, including a birthday invitation from one commander’s wife to another. The writers ignored lives like these. The ground kept them anyway.

cards.headline: The evidence: weighed
learned: Ancient writers had biases
Inscriptions record laws and lives
Coins help date events
Archaeology shows ordinary life

questions.prompt: Which of these was an ancient Roman historian?
questions.explanation: Tacitus, like Livy and Suetonius, was an ancient writer of Roman history.

questions.prompt: Why do historians check ancient writers against other evidence?

options.label: The writers had their own purposes and biases
Latin can no longer be read
Only emperors were allowed to write

questions.explanation: Writers had sources, purposes and biases, so inscriptions, coins and archaeology act as checks.

questions.prompt: From Level 79: what did archaeologists find at Vindolanda?
questions.explanation: More than a thousand wooden tablets from Vindolanda preserve letters, including a birthday invitation.

levels.title: Integration: The Arc of Roman History
levels.objective: After this level you can connect the major turning points of Roman history into one story.
levels.summary: From 753 BCE to 1453 CE, Rome went from kings to republic to empire to a Christian, divided state. One thread: control of the army.

cards.headline: Two thousand years in one story. Ready?
cards.body: More than 2,000 years, six dates, and one pattern that ties them together.

events.label: Traditional founding of Rome
The Republic begins
Octavian becomes Augustus
Under Trajan, the empire reaches its greatest extent
The last western emperor is deposed
Constantinople falls to the Ottoman Turks

cards.headline: The thread through it all
cards.body: Now the pattern. Again and again, whoever controlled the army controlled the state. After Marius, soldiers looked to their general, not the Senate, for pay and for land when they retired. So their loyalty followed the paymaster. Sulla marched his army on Rome. Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his. Vespasian, a general, won a civil war and a throne. In Rome, the road to power ran through the camp.

cards.fact: Roman history spans more than 2,000 years.
cards.context: It runs from the traditional founding in 753 BCE to the fall of Constantinople in 1453 CE. From Iron Age huts on the Palatine Hill to a capital on the Bosporus: that’s the whole story you’ve just walked through.

cards.headline: The arc: complete
learned: Rome was founded, by tradition, in 753 BCE
The Republic began in 509 BCE
Augustus ruled from 27 BCE
The army was the key to power

questions.prompt: Which came first?

options.label: The empire reaches its greatest extent

questions.explanation: The Republic began in 509 BCE, centuries before the others.

questions.prompt: What pattern links Sulla, Caesar and Vespasian?

options.label: Each was elected by the plebeians
Each was killed by his own guard
Each rose to power with a loyal army

questions.explanation: Whoever controlled the army controlled the state; each used soldiers loyal to him.

questions.prompt: From Level 1: Roman history is usually split into three eras. Which list is in the right order?

options.label: Kingdom, Empire, Republic
options.rationale: The Republic came before the Empire.

questions.explanation: Kings, then the Republic from 509 BCE, then the Empire from 27 BCE.

levels.title: Mastery Challenge: Ancient Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Ancient Rome Levels 1–99 across the whole tree.
levels.summary: Questions from across the tree: legends and kings, the Republic, Carthage, Caesar and Augustus, emperors, daily life and the late empire.

cards.headline: The Ancient Rome Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Ten questions from across the whole tree, from a she-wolf and two abandoned twins to a sultan at the walls of Constantinople. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Ancient Rome: mastered
learned: Legends, kings and the Republic
Carthage, Caesar and Augustus
Emperors and everyday life
The late empire and its legacy

questions.prompt: According to legend, what raised the twins Romulus and Remus?
questions.explanation: Legend said the abandoned twins were nursed by a she-wolf.

questions.prompt: Why did the Republic elect two consuls for one-year terms?

options.label: One ruled Rome and one the provinces
So no one person held power for long
Because one always died in battle
options.rationale: The reason was limits on power.

questions.explanation: Two colleagues who could block each other, for one year only, kept anyone from supreme power.

questions.prompt: What did a tribune do by declaring “Veto”?
questions.explanation: A tribune could block another magistrate’s act by saying “Veto,” “I forbid.”

questions.prompt: How did Hannibal win at Cannae?

options.label: He attacked at night with elephants

questions.explanation: His center fell back while his wings and cavalry closed around the Romans: a double envelopment.

questions.prompt: What happened in 27 BCE?

options.label: Caesar crossed the Rubicon with an army
Vesuvius buried the town of Pompeii

questions.explanation: In 27 BCE the Senate gave Octavian the name Augustus, and the Empire began.

questions.prompt: What preserved everyday life at Pompeii?

options.label: A Roman law protecting the town
A flood of mud from the Tiber

questions.explanation: Meters of ash and pumice buried Pompeii in 79 CE, preserving buildings and objects.

questions.prompt: How did aqueducts carry water without pumps?
questions.explanation: Aqueducts ran on a gentle, steady downhill slope, so gravity moved the water.

questions.prompt: Why did Caracalla’s grant of 212 CE matter?

options.label: It ended slavery across the empire
It moved the capital to the East
Almost every free person became a citizen

questions.explanation: Caracalla extended citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire.

questions.prompt: What links Marius’s reforms to Caesar crossing the Rubicon?

options.label: Both were approved by the Senate
Both happened during the Punic Wars

questions.explanation: Marius’s landless soldiers looked to their general; Caesar’s army followed him across the Rubicon.

questions.prompt: How did Christianity’s status change from 313 to 380 CE?

options.label: From tolerated to the official religion

questions.explanation: The Edict of Milan tolerated Christianity in 313 CE; under Theodosius it became official in 380 CE.

levels.title: Money in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the three jobs money does: a way to pay, a measure of value and a way to save.
levels.summary: Money is anything that does three jobs: a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value. In a WWII prison camp, cigarettes did all three.

cards.headline: In a WWII prison camp, cigarettes became money. Even non-smokers wanted them.
cards.body: Economist R. A. Radford was a prisoner there, and in 1945 he explained why. Cigarettes were doing the three jobs that make something money. Learn those three jobs and you know what money is.

cards.headline: Job 1: a way to pay
cards.body: Trade in the camp began as barter: my jam for your biscuits, if we each wanted what the other had. Then cigarettes took over. Everyone, non-smokers included, would sell for cigarettes, because they could spend them later on something else. That's a medium of exchange: something you accept not to use, but to pass on.

cards.headline: Job 2: a measure of value
cards.body: Soon every price in camp was quoted in cigarettes. Prisoners called out offers like "cheese for seven", and laundry cost two cigarettes a garment. Nobody had to work out what cheese was worth in jam. One common unit let anyone compare anything. That's a unit of account, the ruler you measure value with. Yours is probably dollars, euros or pounds.

mascot.line: A savings account you can accidentally smoke. Not ideal, financially speaking.

cards.fact: Money you can smoke is a risky way to save.
cards.context: Job 3 is store of value: money should keep until you're ready to spend it. Prisoners did save cigarettes in reserve. The flaw? People also smoked them. When deliveries stopped, stocks ran out and prices fell. The camp's savings had literally gone up in smoke.

cards.headline: Money: defined
learned: Money does three jobs
Medium of exchange: accepted so you can spend it again
Unit of account: the ruler for prices
Store of value: it keeps until you spend it

questions.prompt: Which list names the three jobs money does?

options.label: A way to earn, a way to spend, a way to give
options.rationale: Earning and giving use money, but the three jobs are paying, measuring and saving.

options.label: A way to pay, a measure of value, a way to save
Coins, banknotes and bank balances
options.rationale: Those are forms money takes, not the jobs it does.

options.label: A way to borrow, a way to tax, a way to lend
options.rationale: Those all use money, but they aren't its three jobs.

questions.explanation: Money is a medium of exchange (a way to pay), a unit of account (a measure of value) and a store of value (a way to save).

questions.prompt: Why would a non-smoker in Radford's camp sell food for cigarettes?

options.label: Guards ordered everyone to trade in cigarettes
options.rationale: Nobody ordered it: cigarettes took over through trading.

options.label: Non-smokers planned to take up smoking
options.rationale: They wanted cigarettes to spend, not to smoke.

options.label: They could spend the cigarettes later on something else
Red Cross parcels held nothing but cigarettes
options.rationale: Parcels also held food like jam, biscuits and chocolate.

questions.explanation: Cigarettes had become a medium of exchange: people took them because others would take them in turn.

questions.prompt: A café menu lists every item in dollars. Which camp habit did the same job?

options.label: Saving cigarettes in reserve
options.rationale: That's storing value, the third job.

options.label: Smoking the cigarettes
options.rationale: That uses cigarettes up; it doesn't measure anything.

options.label: Swapping jam directly for biscuits
options.rationale: That's barter, with no common unit.

questions.explanation: Dollars on a menu and cigarettes in the camp both give every price one common unit: they're units of account.

levels.title: Before Money: Barter
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how barter works and why it gets awkward.
levels.summary: Barter means swapping goods directly. It needs a double coincidence of wants, has no common measure of value and makes saving hard. No pure barter economy has ever been described.

cards.headline: You fix cars. You want lunch. You need a farmer with a broken car.
cards.body: No money allowed. Before you can eat, you have to find someone who has food and also needs a mechanic today. Welcome to barter.

cards.headline: The lucky match barter needs
cards.body: Barter means trading one good or service directly for another, no money involved: your repair for their vegetables. It only works when each of you wants what the other has. Economists call that a double coincidence of wants, and it's rarer than it sounds. The farmer with the broken car does exist. Finding him before lunch is another matter.

cards.headline: No ruler, no savings
cards.body: Remember Level 1's three jobs? Barter struggles with them. There's no common ruler: without an agreed measure, every swap sets its own terms, and each deal stands on its own. Saving is hard too. Picture a farmer hoping to buy a tractor in six months with strawberries picked today. By then, they're jam at best.

mascot.line: So barter isn't money's grandparent. It's more like the backup plan when money goes missing.

cards.fact: Nobody has ever described a society that ran on barter alone.
cards.context: The textbook story, going back to Adam Smith, says people bartered first and switched to money once they saw it worked better. In 1985, anthropologist Caroline Humphrey concluded that no pure barter economy has ever been described. Barter is real, though. It tends to happen between people who know each other, or when money runs short: in Level 1's camp, whenever cigarette deliveries stopped, trade slid back toward barter.

cards.headline: Barter: tried and tested
learned: Barter is swapping goods or services directly
It needs a double coincidence of wants
It has no common ruler and makes saving hard
No pure barter economy has ever been described

questions.prompt: What is a double coincidence of wants?

options.label: Two people wanting the same item
options.rationale: Then they'd be competing. Each must want what the other has.

options.label: Each person wants what the other can offer
Paying twice for the same thing
options.rationale: It's about matching wants, not paying twice.

options.label: A trade in which both sides use money
options.rationale: It's the match that barter needs when there's no money.

questions.explanation: Barter only works when each person has something the other wants. That lucky match is a double coincidence of wants.

questions.prompt: Why is it hard to compare values in a barter economy?

options.label: Governments ban traders from posting price lists
options.rationale: No ban needed: barter simply has no shared unit.

options.label: Every good is worth the same as every other
options.rationale: Goods differ in value; barter just can't measure them in one unit.

options.label: No common measure: each swap sets its own terms
Everyone already prices things in gold coins
options.rationale: Coins would be money, which barter doesn't use.

questions.explanation: Without money as a common ruler, each barter deal stands on its own, so there's no single price to compare.

questions.prompt: From Level 1: what happened to trade in Radford's camp when cigarette deliveries stopped?

options.label: Prices soared
options.rationale: Prices fell as cigarettes ran short.

options.label: Nothing changed
options.rationale: With cigarette money running short, trade changed.

options.label: Prisoners switched to gold coins
options.rationale: Trade fell back on direct swaps instead.

questions.explanation: When the money ran short, prisoners went back to swapping goods directly: barter as a backup plan.

levels.title: Shells, Salt and Stones
levels.objective: After this level you can describe early forms of money like cowrie shells and explain why they worked.
levels.summary: Cowrie shells, salt bars and Yap's giant stones all worked as money. Shells were small, durable and hard to fake; Yap's stones changed owners without moving.

cards.headline: Money has been shells, salt and stone wheels wider than a car.
cards.body: None of it was silly. Each one did Level 1's jobs well enough that people trusted it. Here's what made three very different moneys work.

cards.headline: Cowries: money from the sea
cards.body: Cowrie shells were small, light, durable and hard to fake: most of a money wish list. They served as money in parts of Africa, in places until the late 1800s. In China, strings of cowries were used as payments from around 1000 BCE, and the link stuck. Many Chinese characters about money, like those for buy, loan and tax, still contain the ancient symbol for a shell.
cards.callout: 貝 (bei): shell · 買 buy · 貸 loan · 賦 tax

cards.fact: In Ethiopia, bars of salt were money for centuries.
cards.context: They stayed in use right up to the 1930s. Salt had a big advantage: nearly everyone needs it, so nearly everyone would take it. Like Level 1's cigarettes, it was worth something even to people who weren't planning to spend it.

mascot.line: The safest fortune in history: no pickpocket can lift it. Then again, neither can its owner.

cards.headline: Yap: money too big to move
cards.body: On the Pacific island of Yap, money came as stone discs quarried on Palau, hundreds of kilometers away across the sea. The biggest are more than 3.5 meters across, so they rarely went anywhere. When one changed hands, it stayed put, and everyone simply knew who the new owner was. In one story, a stone sank in a storm on the way home. The islanders agreed it still counted.

cards.headline: Early money: sorted
learned: Cowries: small, durable and hard to fake
Chinese money words still contain the shell symbol
Ethiopia used salt bars into the 1930s
Yap's stones changed owners without moving

questions.prompt: What made cowrie shells good money?

options.label: They were small, durable and hard to fake
They were found only in China
options.rationale: They were used as money in Africa as well as Asia.

options.label: Each shell was stamped with a king's mark
options.rationale: No stamps: the shells themselves were hard to fake.

options.label: People could eat them in hard times
options.rationale: Shells aren't food. That's closer to salt's advantage.

questions.explanation: Cowries were small, light, durable and hard to counterfeit, which is most of what money needs.

questions.prompt: How did a big stone on Yap change owners?

options.label: It was rolled on logs to the buyer's house
options.rationale: The big stones rarely moved at all.

options.label: The buyer carved his family's name into it
options.rationale: No mark was needed: everyone simply knew.

options.label: It stayed put; everyone just knew the new owner
It was broken into pieces and shared out
options.rationale: The stones stayed whole and stayed where they were.

questions.explanation: Ownership lived in the islanders' shared knowledge, so a stone could change hands without moving. Even a sunken one still counted.

questions.prompt: Ethiopia's salt bars were like Level 1's camp cigarettes in what way?

options.label: Both were issued by a government mint
options.rationale: Neither was issued by a government; people simply accepted them.

options.label: Both were valued for more than being money
Both carried a royal stamp to prove them
options.rationale: Neither needed a stamp to be accepted.

options.label: Both were too heavy to carry around
options.rationale: That's Yap's stones, not salt bars or cigarettes.

questions.explanation: Salt is something nearly everyone needs, and cigarettes were smoked. Both had value beyond being money.

levels.title: The First Coins
levels.objective: After this level you can explain where the first coins came from and why metal made good money.
levels.summary: The first coins were probably made in Lydia, in modern Turkey, around 650 BCE: electrum lumps of standard weight, stamped so no one had to weigh them.

cards.headline: The first coins probably came from a kingdom you've never heard of.
cards.body: Lydia, in what's now Turkey, around 650 BCE. And the big idea wasn't the metal. People had paid with metal for ages. It was the little picture pressed into it.

cards.headline: The trouble with lumps
cards.body: Before coins, traders paid with rings and bars of gold and silver. Metal made fine money: it's portable, it doesn't rot like Level 2's strawberries, and it's hard to fake. The catch? Every deal meant weighing the metal and checking it. Imagine a set of scales at every checkout.

cards.headline: A stamp you could trust
cards.body: Lydia's coins were lumps of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver, made to strict standard weights. Many carried a lion's head, which seems to have been a royal symbol. The stamp marked the coin as official money that the state would accept as payment. No scales, no testing: you just counted. That's the whole trick of a coin.

mascot.line: Spade-shaped money: finally, a currency you could really dig into.

cards.fact: As rich as Croesus? He's often credited with the first pure gold and silver coins.
cards.context: Electrum mixed metals, so its worth was hard to pin down. Lydia fixed that by minting separate gold and silver coins, often credited to the legendarily wealthy King Croesus, though some were probably made before and after his reign. The idea spread fast around the Mediterranean. Meanwhile, China had its own coins, probably invented independently: bronze, cast in the shapes of spades and knives.

levels.title: Paper Money
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how paper money began in China and spread around the world.
levels.summary: Paper money began in China: Tang merchants' flying money, then Song-era notes in Sichuan, where iron coins were heavy. Europe's first banknotes came from Sweden in 1661.

cards.headline: Paper money was invented because coins were too heavy. Literally.
cards.body: In 11th-century China, and again in 17th-century Sweden, people's coins were so heavy that a paper promise was simply easier to carry.

cards.headline: Flying money
cards.body: It started with merchants in Tang dynasty China (618–907). Rather than haul heavy coins on long journeys, they used paper drafts nicknamed "flying money". Was that the first paper money? The British Museum says yes; other historians call it a draft for moving funds, more like a money order than cash. Either way, paper had started standing in for metal.

mascot.line: Imagine paying for lunch in iron. Suddenly paper looks like genius.

cards.headline: Sichuan's iron problem
cards.body: In 11th-century Sichuan, people used iron coins, which were heavy. So they left their coins on deposit and carried paper certificates instead, which could be spent in their place. Around 1023, the Song government took over issuing them. These notes, called jiaozi, are widely described as the world's first paper currency.

cards.fact: Europe's first real banknotes came from Sweden in 1661.
cards.context: Marco Polo had described China's paper money back in the 13th century. Then Stockholms Banco issued notes, and they caught on for a familiar reason: Sweden's copper coins were heavy and cumbersome. But paper is only a promise. When the public lost confidence in the bank, it failed. Why people trust paper at all is Level 6's question.

levels.title: Why Money Has Value
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why money is valuable because people trust it and accept it.
levels.summary: Today's money is fiat money: legal tender backed by no commodity. A $100 bill costs about 11 cents to print; its value comes from trust that others will accept it.

cards.headline: A $100 bill costs about 11 cents to print. So why is it worth $100?
cards.body: Paper, ink and labor came to about 11 cents a note in the Federal Reserve's 2025 figures. Everything else comes from something you can't see or touch.

cards.headline: Fiat money
cards.body: Look at a US bill. It says: "This note is legal tender for all debts, public and private." Nothing about gold, or anything else behind it. That's fiat money: it has no value of its own, and a government declares it legal tender. Today's dollars are fiat money. Their only backing, as one economics textbook puts it, is shared faith and trust that they have value.

cards.headline: A chain of confidence
cards.body: Picture the chain. A baker takes your bill because her flour supplier will take it from her, and he takes it because his landlord will. Everyone accepts it because everyone else does. It's the logic of Level 1's camp, where non-smokers took cigarettes because others would take them later. Money works because people believe it will.

mascot.line: Money is a story we all agree to believe. Luckily, it's a very useful story.

cards.fact: A stone on the seabed can be money. It all comes down to belief.
cards.context: Remember Level 3's sunken stone on Yap? In 1991, economist Milton Friedman used it to show how much money rests on unquestioned belief, and he meant our money too. The flip side follows. When belief goes, paper is just paper, as Level 5's Swedish bank found out when the public lost confidence.

levels.title: The Gold Standard
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what the gold standard was and why countries left it.
levels.summary: Under a gold standard, money is tied to a fixed amount of gold. Gold's supply couldn't keep pace with growing economies, and the dollar's last gold link ended in 1971.

cards.headline: For generations, a paper note was a ticket you could cash in for gold.
cards.body: Hand over your notes, walk away with metal. Then, country by country, the deal ended. The last big link snapped on August 15, 1971.

cards.headline: Money tied to metal
cards.body: Under a gold standard, a country's unit of money is a fixed amount of gold. Britain adopted one in 1821, and by the 1870s other big economies, including Germany and France, had followed. In the US, the Federal Reserve had to swap dollars for gold at a fixed price. The appeal was simple: paper you could trust, because gold stood behind it.

mascot.line: Imagine your allowance growing only as fast as miners can dig. That's the problem in one picture.

cards.headline: The golden handcuffs
cards.body: The catch: the supply of newly mined gold has nothing to do with how much money a growing economy needs. In hard times, that tied governments' hands. World War I pushed countries off gold, the Great Depression finished the job, and by 1937 no country kept a full gold standard. In 1933, the US stopped swapping money for gold coins and bars at home.

cards.fact: In 1971, Nixon "temporarily" cut the dollar's last link to gold.
cards.context: After World War II, the Bretton Woods system fixed other currencies to the dollar, and dollars to gold at $35 an ounce. Foreign governments could still cash their dollars in. On August 15, 1971, President Nixon said he had told the Treasury to "suspend temporarily" that swap. The system soon ended, and the world's money became fiat money: Level 6's kind, backed by trust.

levels.title: Money as Numbers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why most money today exists only as numbers in bank records.
levels.summary: Most money today is bank deposits, records of what banks owe you. In the UK, 97% of money is deposits. Paying by card just changes two balances.

cards.headline: Most of your money has never been printed.
cards.body: In the UK, 97% of the money people hold isn't notes or coins at all. It's numbers in banks' records. (That's the Bank of England's figure from 2014.)

cards.headline: Your balance is a promise
cards.body: A bank deposit isn't a pile of your cash in a vault. It's a record of what the bank owes you, a kind of IOU. Money today is a special IOU, one that everyone in the economy trusts. That's why most people get paid in deposits, and many never swap them back into cash.

mascot.line: Somewhere, a computer changed two numbers so you could have coffee. Romantic, really.

cards.headline: Paying without anything moving
cards.body: Pay for a coffee by debit card and no cash travels anywhere. The banks just edit two numbers: your balance goes down and the café's goes up. The payment is the change to the record. You used your deposit as money without ever touching a coin.

cards.fact: Yap's islanders would find your bank account oddly familiar.
cards.context: On Level 3's Yap, a stone could change owners without moving. In the early 1930s, the New York Fed did much the same with gold: rather than ship it across the ocean to the Bank of France, it moved bars into drawers in its own vault labeled as French. Milton Friedman, who told both stories, pointed out that most of our wealth, bank balances included, is something we never actually see.

levels.title: Cryptocurrency
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what cryptocurrencies are and how they differ from money in a bank.
levels.summary: Cryptocurrencies like bitcoin are digital tokens recorded on a blockchain, a shared ledger kept by a network. With a nearly fixed supply, bitcoin's price swings sharply.

cards.headline: Bitcoin has no bank, no boss and no building. So who keeps the books?
cards.body: Level 8's money lives in a bank's records. Bitcoin's records are kept by a whole network of computers at once, with no bank, company or government in charge.

cards.headline: Money without a middleman
cards.body: In October 2008, someone calling themselves Satoshi Nakamoto proposed bitcoin: a digital currency that wouldn't rely on banks or governments. It launched in 2009, and nobody knows for sure who Nakamoto is. Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, named for its heavy use of cryptography, the mathematics of codes. There are no bitcoin coins or notes. It exists only as entries in its own records.

cards.headline: A ledger everyone holds
cards.body: Those records form a blockchain: a ledger of transactions shared across the network. Transactions are bundled into blocks, and each block carries a cryptographic fingerprint of the one before. Change an old entry and every later link breaks, so tampering is easy to spot. To spend, you sign with a secret private key. Lose it and the coins are gone for good. Researchers have compared all this to Level 3's Yap, whose islanders kept a shared record of who owned each stone.

cards.fact: Bitcoin's price can skyrocket or tumble within days.
cards.context: Its price is set by supply and demand, and the supply is capped at just under 21 million coins. With supply more or less fixed, every swing in demand lands on the price: a cousin of Level 7's gold problem. Supporters see that fixed supply as a hedge against inflation. Critics, including the European Central Bank, say the swings make it too unstable to be Level 1's store of value.

levels.title: Checkpoint: What Money Is
levels.objective: After this level you can trace money from barter and coins to digital money, and explain what gives it value.
levels.summary: Useful money is durable, portable, divisible, uniform, limited in supply and acceptable. From shells to bitcoin, every money has rested on trust.

cards.headline: Shells, stones, coins, paper, records, code. Which makes the best money?
cards.body: Chapter 1 has walked you through money in all its costumes. Economists have a scorecard for judging them. Time to use it.

cards.headline: The six-trait test
cards.body: Useful money is durable (it lasts), portable (easy to carry), divisible (splits into small amounts), uniform (each unit is as good as another), limited in supply (hard to make more of) and acceptable (people take it). That last one is Level 6's whole story: acceptance rests on trust.

items.label: Yap stones
points: Not portable: the biggest are over 3.5 m wide

items.label: A US $20 bill
points: Scores well on all six traits

cards.headline: One thread from shells to code
cards.body: Money kept changing shape: shells and salt, Lydia's stamped coins, China's paper, gold-backed notes, bank records, bitcoin's blockchain. What stayed the same were Level 1's three jobs, and the thing under them all: people accept money because they trust others will too. Money works because people believe it will.

levels.title: Your Cosmic Address
levels.objective: After this level you can state Earth's address: third planet from the Sun, a star in the Milky Way.
levels.summary: The Sun is a star, Earth is planet three, and our whole solar system lives in the Milky Way.

cards.headline: Every star you see at night is a sun. Ours is just the closest one.
cards.body: That little twinkle you wish on? It's a sun. It looks tiny for one reason only: it's unbelievably far away.

cards.headline: Your cosmic mailing address
cards.body: If aliens wanted to mail you a postcard, they'd need a long address. Line one: Earth. Line two: the third planet from the Sun, with two neighbors closer in and five farther out. Line three: the solar system, which is just the Sun plus everything swinging around it. And we're not done yet.

mascot.line: You're always seeing the Sun a little late. I've been late my whole life, so this one I love.

cards.fact: The Sun you see is 8 minutes old.
cards.context: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us, so the Sun in the sky is the Sun from 8 minutes ago. If it vanished right now, you'd keep seeing it for about 8 more minutes. Light is the fastest thing there is. The Sun is just that far away.

cards.headline: Last line: the Milky Way
cards.body: The final line on the envelope is the Milky Way, a spiral of at least 100 billion stars. We live out in the suburbs, about 26,000 light-years from downtown. On a dark night, that hazy stripe across the sky is the rest of our galaxy. You're looking at your own neighborhood from the sidewalk.

levels.title: The Sun, Up Close
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what powers the Sun and how dominant it is in the solar system.
levels.summary: The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, holds 99.8% of the solar system's mass, and is about 4.6 billion years old.

cards.headline: The Sun isn't on fire. It's doing something far stranger.
cards.body: Picture the Sun as a giant bonfire? Wrong picture. It has been shining for about 4.6 billion years, and no fire lasts that long. Something much stranger is going on inside.

cards.headline: A star that squeezes atoms
cards.body: Deep in the Sun's core it's about 15 million °C. At that heat, hydrogen atoms slam together so hard that they fuse into helium, and every crash releases a tiny spark of energy. One spark is nothing. But the core does this an almost unimaginable number of times every second, and all those sparks add up to every bit of sunshine you've ever felt.

cards.fact: The Sun holds about 99.8% of the solar system's mass.
cards.context: Every planet, moon, asteroid and comet put together? That's the other 0.2%. We're the crumbs. If the Sun were as tall as your front door, Earth would be about the size of a nickel. No wonder everything circles it: the Sun's gravity is what holds the whole solar system together.

cards.headline: Middle-aged, not old
cards.body: 4.6 billion years sounds ancient, until you learn that a star like ours can keep fusing hydrogen for about 10 billion years. So the Sun isn't old at all. It's middle-aged, with billions of good years of shining still ahead of it.

levels.title: The Rocky Four
levels.objective: After this level you can name the rocky planets and explain why Venus, not Mercury, is the hottest.
levels.summary: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are rocky. Venus is the hottest planet thanks to its heat-trapping atmosphere, and Mars is red because of rust.

cards.headline: Mercury is closest to the Sun. So why is Venus hotter?
cards.body: You'd bet on Mercury, right? It's the closest planet to the Sun. You'd lose that bet. The winner is hiding under a thick blanket next door.

cards.headline: The rocky four
cards.body: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are small worlds of rock and metal. You could stand on any of them. You wouldn't enjoy most of them. Take Mercury: about 430 °C in the day, then about −180 °C at night. It's the closest planet to the Sun, and it still can't keep warm.

cards.headline: Venus: a runaway greenhouse
cards.body: Venus wears a thick blanket of carbon dioxide. Sunlight gets in, but the heat can't get back out, so it piles up. The result is a surface over 450 °C, hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun. The air is so heavy that the pressure on the ground is about 90 times Earth's. Mercury gets the sunshine. Venus keeps the heat.

cards.fact: Mars is red because it's rusty.
cards.context: Seriously. Iron oxide, the same stuff as the rust on an old bike, coats Martian dust and rocks, and fine red dust in the air tints the whole planet. That air is thin, too: less than 1% of Earth's air pressure. Venus's air would crush you. Mars's barely shows up.

levels.title: Giants of the Outer Dark
levels.objective: After this level you can tell gas giants from ice giants and describe Jupiter's and Saturn's standout features.
levels.summary: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. Jupiter outweighs every other planet combined, and Saturn's rings are mostly ice.

cards.headline: Past Mars, the planets stop being rocky and start being enormous.
cards.body: Level 3's four worlds were small and rocky. Past Mars, the rules change. The next four planets are giants, and you couldn't land on a single one of them.

cards.fact: Jupiter has more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined.
cards.context: Remember the crumbs from Level 2, the 0.2% of the solar system that isn't the Sun? Jupiter is the biggest crumb by far. Put it on one side of a giant scale and every other planet on the other side. Jupiter wins. Double the pile and Jupiter still wins. If the planets were a team, Jupiter would be carrying it.

cards.headline: Saturn's rings are ice
cards.body: Those famous rings aren't a solid hoop you could walk around on. They're countless separate chunks of water ice, with a little rock mixed in. Some are as small as specks of dust. Others are as big as a house. So Saturn's rings are basically a giant field of hail. Some of the ice cubes are just the size of your home.

levels.title: Why We Have Seasons
levels.objective: After this level you can explain that seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun.
levels.summary: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. Each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun, which is why seasons are opposite north and south.

cards.headline: Most people get this one wrong: summer isn't when Earth is closest to the Sun.
cards.body: It's the obvious guess: summer is hot because Earth swings closer to the Sun. Nice guess. The calendar disagrees.

cards.fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
cards.context: That's the middle of winter in the Northern Hemisphere. If distance ran the seasons, New Year's Day would be beach weather in New York. Instead, northern summer arrives when Earth is farther from the Sun. So distance can't be what makes summer. Something else is in charge.

cards.headline: It's the tilt
cards.body: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. When your half of the planet leans toward the Sun, sunlight hits the ground more directly and days last longer, so more energy lands on each patch of ground. That's summer. Lean away, and the same sunlight arrives at a slant and spreads thin, like a flashlight beam tipped across a table. That's winter. Same Sun, different angle.

cards.headline: Opposite seasons
cards.body: Here's the proof it's the lean. The two hemispheres tilt opposite ways, so they take turns. In December, New York shivers while Sydney has summer. In July it flips: summer up north, winter in Australia. Same planet, same trip around the Sun, opposite seasons. Somewhere on Earth, someone is always wearing a scarf.

cards.headline: Seasons: solved
learned: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°
Tilt, not distance, causes seasons
Earth is closest to the Sun in January
The hemispheres have opposite seasons

levels.title: The Moon's Changing Face
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Moon phases and why we only ever see one side of the Moon.
levels.summary: Phases show how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces us, over a ~29.5-day cycle. The Moon is tidally locked, so the same side always faces Earth.

cards.headline: The Moon doesn't change shape. You're just seeing it from a different angle.
cards.body: Tonight a thin crescent, next week a full circle. The Moon seems to grow and shrink, but it's the same Moon the whole time. What changes is how you're looking at it.

cards.headline: Half lit, always
cards.body: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that sunlit half: a thin crescent, a half, the full face, then back again. Nothing is covering the Moon; only our viewing angle changes. Try it with a lamp and a ball held at arm's length, turning slowly, and you'll get phases in your living room.
cards.callout: One full cycle of phases: about 29.5 days

cards.fact: We always see the same side of the Moon.
cards.context: The Moon is tidally locked: it rotates exactly once per orbit, so the same face always points at us. Walk a circle around a chair while always facing it, and you'll have turned all the way around once too. And the 'dark side'? Not dark at all. The far side gets as much sunlight as the near side. We just never get to see it from Earth.

cards.headline: Moon: decoded

The Moon is tidally locked

levels.title: Eclipses and a Cosmic Coincidence
levels.objective: After this level you can tell solar from lunar eclipses and explain why the Moon can exactly cover the Sun.
levels.summary: A solar eclipse is the Moon blocking the Sun; a lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow on the Moon. The Sun is ~400× wider and ~400× farther than the Moon.

cards.headline: By pure luck, the Moon is exactly the right size to blot out the Sun.
cards.body: The Sun is enormous and the Moon is small, yet the Moon can cover the Sun completely. It isn't design. It's a coincidence of two numbers.

cards.headline: Two kinds of eclipse: who's blocking whom?

items.label: Solar eclipse
points: The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth
The Moon's shadow falls on Earth
Only happens at new Moon, when the Moon sits on the Sun's side of us

items.label: Lunar eclipse
points: Earth passes between the Sun and Moon
Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
Only happens at full Moon, when the Moon is on the far side of us

cards.fact: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, and about 400 times farther away.
cards.context: Those two numbers cancel out, so the Sun and Moon look almost exactly the same size in our sky. It's the same trick as hiding a faraway building behind your thumb. That's why, in a total solar eclipse, the Moon can cover the Sun's bright disc and reveal its faint outer glow, the corona. The Sun is 400 times bigger. It's also 400 times farther. Tie.

cards.headline: Eclipses: explained
learned: Solar eclipse: the Moon blocks the Sun
Lunar eclipse: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
The 400× coincidence makes total solar eclipses possible

options.label: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon

questions.prompt: Why can the Moon exactly cover the Sun during a total solar eclipse?

options.label: The Moon and Sun are actually the same size
options.rationale: The Sun is about 400 times wider.

options.label: The Moon is closer to the Sun

questions.explanation: The Sun's extra size is balanced by its extra distance, so both look about the same size from Earth.

levels.title: Light-Years: Measuring the Unmeasurable
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a light-year measures and how far the nearest star is.
levels.summary: A light-year is a distance: about 9.46 trillion km. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

cards.headline: A light-year sounds like a unit of time. It isn't.
cards.body: It has 'year' right there in the name, so it's a fair guess. But a light-year is a ruler, not a clock.

cards.headline: Distance, measured in light
cards.body: A light-year is how far light travels in one year: about 9.46 trillion kilometers. So it's a distance, the way a mile is. Kilometers are great for a road trip. Out among the stars they pile up into numbers nobody can read, so astronomers switched to a bigger ruler.

cards.headline: Why measure space in light?
cards.body: Light is the fastest thing there is, which makes it a handy measuring tape. It crosses from the Moon to Earth in just over a second. From the Sun, it takes about 8 minutes (Level 1's slightly late Sun). So the Moon is about one light-second away and the Sun about 8 light-minutes. Past the Sun, even light needs years, and the ruler grows to match.

cards.fact: The closest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away.
cards.context: So its light takes about 4.2 years to reach us. Moon: a second. Sun: 8 minutes. Next star: more than four years. And that's the closest one; every other star is even farther. Proxima is our next-door neighbor. The street is just very, very long.

levels.title: The Life of a Star
levels.objective: After this level you can read a star's temperature from its color and outline how the Sun will end.
levels.summary: Stars are born in clouds of gas and dust. Blue stars are hottest, red coolest. The Sun will become a red giant and then a white dwarf; massive stars can go supernova.

cards.headline: Stars have a life story: birth, a long middle age, and a very dramatic ending.
cards.body: Level 2 told you the Sun is middle-aged. So what comes next? Here's the Sun's whole story, plus a trick for reading any star's temperature just by its color.

cards.headline: Color is temperature
cards.body: Look closely and stars have colors, and each color is a thermometer reading. Blue stars are the hottest; red stars are the coolest. That's backwards from your kitchen tap, where red means hot. The Sun sits in the middle: it shines white from space, and our air scatters away some of its blue light, so it looks yellowish from the ground.

cards.headline: The Sun's life, in four stops

events.label: Born from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust
Middle-aged, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core
Runs low on hydrogen in its core and swells into a red giant
Sheds its outer layers and ends as a white dwarf

cards.headline: Bigger stars, bigger endings
cards.body: Relax: the Sun won't explode. It isn't massive enough. Stars much more massive than the Sun get a far louder exit: a supernova, an explosion that can briefly outshine a whole galaxy. Picture one dying star, for a moment, brighter than every other star in its galaxy put together. The Sun's quiet ending sounds better already.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Your Place in the Universe
levels.objective: After this level you can trace Earth's address from our planet all the way out to the observable universe.
levels.summary: The Milky Way is ~100,000 light-years across, Andromeda is ~2.5 million light-years away, and the observable universe holds billions of galaxies in a ~13.8-billion-year-old cosmos.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale. Let's zoom all the way out.
cards.body: Remember the cosmic mailing address from Level 1? Earth, the solar system, the Milky Way. Time to find out how big that last line is, and what lies beyond it.

cards.headline: Our galaxy
cards.body: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across. A light-year is a distance, so light leaving one edge would take about 100,000 years to reach the other. In Level 8, Proxima Centauri at 4.2 light-years felt far. Our galaxy is more than 20,000 times wider than that. The suburbs are big.

cards.fact: Andromeda, the nearest large spiral galaxy, is about 2.5 million light-years away.
cards.context: You could line up 25 Milky Ways in that gap. Yet on a dark night you can see Andromeda with the naked eye, as a faint smudge. That smudge is a whole galaxy, and the light reaching your eye took about 2.5 million years to get here.

cards.headline: And then everything else
cards.body: Andromeda is just one galaxy. The observable universe holds billions of galaxies, many with billions of stars each. And the universe itself is about 13.8 billion years old, about three times the Sun's age. So here's the full address: one planet, around one star, in one galaxy among billions.

levels.title: Why the Sky Turns
levels.objective: After this level you can explain that day and night, and the stars rising and setting, come from Earth spinning.
levels.summary: Earth spins once a day from west to east, so the Sun and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

cards.headline: The sky isn't turning. You are.
cards.body: Every sunrise looks like the Sun climbing up to meet you. It isn't going anywhere. Your patch of Earth is rolling toward it, and all night long the stars play the very same trick.

cards.headline: One spin, one day
cards.body: Earth spins on its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, about once every 24 hours. At any moment, the half facing the Sun has day and the half facing away has night. Nobody switches the Sun off at bedtime. Earth's spin simply carries your side of the planet from the sunny half into the dark one, and back again by breakfast.

cards.headline: Why everything rises in the east
cards.body: Earth spins from west to east, so your eastern horizon turns toward the Sun first. From where you stand, the Sun seems to climb up in the east and sink in the west. The Moon, the planets and the stars do exactly the same, for exactly the same reason. They aren't parading around us. Earth's spin sweeps them all across the sky the same way, like scenery sliding past a train window.

cards.fact: At the equator, Earth's surface moves at about 1,670 km/h.
cards.context: So why don't you feel it? Because you, the ground and the air all move together at a steady speed. Nothing rushes past you, so there's no wind in your hair and no coffee in your lap. The whole planet is one very smooth ride.

cards.headline: Daily spin: understood

levels.title: A Year Around the Sun
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a year is, why leap years exist, and why the night sky changes with the seasons.
levels.summary: A year is one orbit of about 365.25 days. The quarter-days add up to leap days, and the night sky shifts as we orbit.

cards.headline: A year is just one lap.
cards.body: Every birthday, you've ridden once around the Sun since the last one. The candles on your cake are really a lap counter.

cards.headline: One lap, one year
cards.body: Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once, and that lap is what we call a year. It's no gentle stroll, either. Earth races along its orbit at about 30 km every second. Count to ten and you've traveled about 300 km through space, without ever leaving your chair.

cards.headline: Where the quarter-days go
cards.body: Calendars count 365 days, but each orbit takes about 365.25. That spare quarter of a day looks harmless, yet it piles up: after four years, the calendar is a whole day behind Earth. So about every four years we add February 29 to catch up and keep the calendar in step with the seasons. Leap day is the calendar settling its debts.

cards.headline: A different night sky each season
cards.body: At night, your side of Earth faces away from the Sun, out into space. As Earth moves along its orbit, that night-time view swings toward different parts of space, so each season gets its own constellations. That's why Orion is a winter evening sight in the Northern Hemisphere. The view out of the back window changes as you go around the track.

options.label: To keep the calendar in step with the Moon
options.rationale: Leap days track Earth’s orbit around the Sun, not the Moon.

options.label: Because February is too short
options.rationale: February is just where the extra day goes.

questions.explanation: A year is about 365.25 days. The extra quarter-days add up to about one day every four years, so leap years add February 29.

questions.prompt: From Level 5: seasons repeat every year. What happens during one orbit to cause them?

options.label: Earth moves much closer to the Sun, then farther away
options.rationale: Distance isn’t the cause; Earth is closest in January.

options.label: The Sun gets hotter, then cooler
options.rationale: The Sun’s output barely changes over a year.

options.rationale: Earth’s spin rate stays essentially the same.

questions.explanation: Earth’s axis stays tilted the same way as it orbits, so over one year each hemisphere leans toward the Sun (summer) and then away from it (winter).

levels.title: Connect the Dots: Constellations
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a constellation is and why its stars usually aren’t near each other.
levels.summary: There are 88 official constellations covering the sky. Their stars only line up from our viewpoint.

cards.headline: Orion isn't really a hunter, and his stars aren't even neighbors.
cards.body: A constellation is a picture we see from one spot in space: Earth. So what's actually up there?

cards.headline: From pictures to borders
cards.body: People have long joined up the stars into patterns and named them after figures, animals and objects. Today astronomers go further: the sky is divided into 88 official constellations, each one a region with set boundaries, like countries on a map. Together they cover the whole sky, so every star lands in some constellation, even the ones that aren't part of any picture.

cards.headline: A trick of perspective
cards.body: Stars that look side by side can be very different distances from Earth. Remember light-years from Level 8? One star in a pattern could be a few dozen light-years away, its neighbor hundreds. They only look close together from where we stand, the way a faraway streetlight can seem to sit right next to your neighbor's porch light.

cards.fact: The Big Dipper is not a constellation.
cards.context: It's an asterism: a familiar star pattern that isn't one of the official constellations. The Dipper is part of the constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear. So if you've ever spotted the saucepan, congratulations: you've also seen part of a bear.

cards.headline: Constellations: decoded
learned: Constellations began as named star patterns
There are 88 official constellations
Their stars are usually far apart in space

options.rationale: That’s the number of zodiac signs; the constellations cover the whole sky.

questions.explanation: Astronomers officially recognize 88 constellations, which together cover the entire sky.

options.label: They are the same age

options.label: Their light reaches us at the same moment it leaves

options.label: The farther star’s light left it about 450 years earlier

questions.explanation: A light-year is how far light travels in a year. Light from a star 500 light-years away left it about 500 years ago; from 50 light-years, about 50 years ago.

levels.title: The North Star
levels.objective: After this level you can find north with Polaris and explain why some stars never set.
levels.summary: Polaris sits above the North Pole, so it stays put while the sky wheels around it. Its height gives your latitude.

cards.headline: One star barely moves all night. Find it, and you've found north.
cards.body: Watch the sky for a few hours and the stars wheel slowly around. All but one, which sits almost still, as if the whole sky were pinned to it.

cards.headline: The star above the pole
cards.body: That star is Polaris, the North Star, and it lies almost directly above Earth's North Pole. As Earth spins, every other star circles around it while Polaris stays nearly fixed, like the hub of a turning wheel. Face it and you're facing north. One surprise: it isn't the brightest star in the sky. That's Sirius. Polaris is famous for where it sits, not how it shines.

cards.headline: Stars that never set
cards.body: From mid-northern latitudes, stars close to Polaris trace small circles around it that never dip below the horizon. They're called circumpolar stars. While the rest of the sky rises and sets, these never leave: their circles around the pole stay above the horizon all night. And Polaris doubles as a free GPS. Its height above your horizon, in degrees, roughly equals your latitude.

cards.fact: Polaris won't be the North Star forever.
cards.context: Earth's axis slowly wobbles like a spinning top, tracing a circle about every 26,000 years, so over the ages the pole points at different stars. The Southern Hemisphere already knows the feeling: it has no bright pole star at all, so navigators there have used the Southern Cross to find south.

cards.headline: North: found
learned: Polaris sits almost directly above the North Pole

options.label: Their circles around the pole stay above the horizon

options.label: They only rise during the long winter nights

questions.explanation: Earth’s spin makes every star appear to circle the pole. Stars close to Polaris trace circles small enough to stay above the horizon all night.

levels.title: The Ecliptic: The Planets’ Highway
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Sun, Moon and planets all travel along the same narrow band of sky.
levels.summary: The ecliptic is the Sun’s yearly path. The Moon and planets stay near it because the solar system is flat.

cards.headline: The planets don't roam the whole sky. They stick to one narrow road.
cards.body: The Sun, the Moon and every planet keep to the same slim strip of sky. It's no coincidence. It's a clue to the shape of the solar system.

cards.headline: The Sun's yearly path
cards.body: As Earth orbits, the Sun seems to drift slowly against the background stars, and after a year it's back where it started. The path the Sun appears to follow across the sky over a year is called the ecliptic. The zodiac constellations lie along it, plus a 13th that tradition leaves out: Ophiuchus. Sorry, Ophiuchus.
cards.callout: Ecliptic = the Sun's path over a year

cards.headline: A flat solar system
cards.body: Why does everything use the same road? The planets all orbit the Sun in nearly the same flat plane, and the Moon's orbit lies close to it too. Hold a dinner plate edge-on at eye level and everything on it lines up in a thin line. We're looking at the solar system edge-on from inside, and that line is the ecliptic. So a bright "star" near where the Sun set may well be a planet.

cards.fact: Eclipses can only happen when the Moon is on the ecliptic.
cards.context: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to the ecliptic, so most months the new Moon passes just above or below the Sun's path. Near miss. Only when a new or full Moon lands close to where the two paths cross do we get an eclipse.

cards.headline: Planetary highway: mapped
learned: The ecliptic is the Sun’s path over a year
Zodiac constellations lie along it

options.label: Their orbits lie in nearly the same flat plane as Earth’s

options.rationale: Darkness has nothing to do with it.

options.rationale: Planets orbit the Sun, not Earth.

questions.explanation: The solar system is flat: the planets orbit in nearly the same plane as Earth, so from Earth they all appear close to the Sun’s path.

questions.prompt: From Level 7: there’s a new Moon every month. Why isn’t there a solar eclipse every month?

options.label: The Moon is too far away to cover the Sun most months

options.rationale: In a solar eclipse it’s the Moon’s shadow that matters.

options.label: The Moon usually passes just above or below the Sun’s path

questions.explanation: The Moon’s orbit is slightly tilted to the ecliptic. Most new Moons pass above or below the Sun; only a line-up on the ecliptic gives a solar eclipse.

levels.title: Wanderers: How Planets Move Across the Sky
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why planets drift against the stars and sometimes appear to loop backwards.
levels.summary: Planets drift against the stars as they orbit. When Earth overtakes an outer planet, it seems to go backwards: retrograde motion.

cards.headline: Every few years, Mars seems to stop, reverse and loop back across the sky.
cards.body: It never actually turns around. You're watching from a moving planet, and that changes what you see.

cards.headline: The wanderers
cards.body: Night after night, the stars hold their patterns. Planets don't: they slowly shift position against the background stars as they orbit the Sun, always keeping to the ecliptic road from Level 15. The ancient Greeks noticed these drifting lights, and the word "planet" comes from their word for "wanderer." The stars stay put; the planets go for a stroll.

cards.headline: Overtaking on the inside lane
cards.body: Earth orbits closer to the Sun than Mars does, and it moves faster. Every so often Earth, on its faster inner orbit, catches up with Mars and overtakes it. For a while, Mars appears to slide backwards against the stars, then it carries on forward. You've seen this on the highway: pass a slower car and it seems to drift backwards, though you're both going forward.

cards.fact: Retrograde motion is only apparent.
cards.context: No planet ever reverses direction in its orbit. The backwards loop is a change in our viewpoint, not in the planet's path. Mars has no idea it's doing anything strange.

cards.headline: Wanderers: explained

options.rationale: Mercury orbits inside Earth’s orbit, so Earth never overtakes it.

options.label: Venus
options.rationale: Venus orbits inside Earth’s orbit and moves faster than Earth.

options.label: Earth

questions.explanation: Mars is the rocky planet just outside Earth’s orbit. Earth overtakes it every couple of years, causing its retrograde loop.

levels.title: Tides: The Moon’s Pull on the Ocean
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why most coasts get two high tides a day and what spring and neap tides are.
levels.summary: The Moon’s gravity makes two bulges of ocean water. Earth spins through both each day; the Sun makes tides bigger or smaller.

cards.headline: The Moon moves oceans. Twice a day.
cards.body: Every beach you've ever visited is being tugged by the Moon. The odd part is that most coasts get two high tides a day, not one.

cards.headline: Two bulges, not one
cards.body: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans and stretches them into two bulges: one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side of Earth. Earth spins through both bulges, so most coastlines get two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours and 50 minutes. High tide isn't the sea coming to visit. It's your beach passing under a bulge.

cards.headline: The Sun joins in
cards.body: The Sun pulls on the oceans too, just more weakly than the Moon. Around new and full Moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up and their pulls combine: extra-high highs and extra-low lows, called spring tides. Around the quarter Moons, the Sun and Moon pull at right angles and the tides are gentler: neap tides. Teamwork makes big tides.

cards.fact: Spring tides have nothing to do with spring.
cards.context: They happen twice a month, all year round, including the middle of winter. They follow the Moon's phases, not the calendar. Blame the name, not the season.

levels.title: Where the Moon Came From
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the giant-impact explanation for the Moon’s origin and the evidence for it.
levels.summary: The Moon most likely formed from debris after a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.

cards.headline: The Moon may be made of pieces of Earth.
cards.body: The leading explanation starts with a crash between the young Earth and a whole Mars-sized world. The Moon is what the crash left behind.

cards.headline: The giant impact
cards.body: About 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body that scientists call Theia is thought to have slammed into the young Earth. The collision flung debris out around Earth, and that debris gathered to form the Moon. Remember the Sun's age from Level 2, about 4.6 billion years? The Moon showed up early in the story, not long after Earth itself. Earth's worst day, and it got a Moon out of it.

cards.headline: The clues
cards.body: How do you check a crash nobody saw? Start with the Moon rocks Apollo astronauts brought back: they're chemically very similar to rocks from Earth's mantle. The Moon also has only a small iron core compared with Earth. And when scientists run computer simulations of a giant impact, out comes a Moon with an Earth-like makeup and a small iron core. Not proof, but every clue points the same way: back to Earth.

cards.headline: Moon origin: reconstructed

levels.title: Craters and Seas on the Moon
levels.objective: After this level you can explain where lunar craters and the dark “seas” came from and why they last so long.
levels.summary: Craters are impact scars preserved for billions of years; the dark maria are ancient hardened lava.

cards.headline: The "Man in the Moon" is made of ancient lava.
cards.body: Look at a full Moon and you see a face. Look again and you're reading billions of years of history, written in lava and craters.

cards.headline: Scars that never heal
cards.body: The Moon's craters were blasted out by asteroids and comets, and they range from tiny pits to basins hundreds of kilometers across. What's surprising is how long they last. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, no liquid water and no plate tectonics. Nothing wears its craters away, so they survive for billions of years. Every hit the Moon has taken, from the smallest pit to the biggest basin, is still on the record. The Moon never tidies up.
cards.callout: No air, no water, no erasing

cards.headline: Seas without water
cards.body: The dark patches are called maria, Latin for "seas." They're vast plains of ancient lava that cooled and hardened: seas of rock, named for water that was never there. Most maria sit on the near side, the side that always faces Earth. So the "Man in the Moon" isn't just a face. He's a face that's always turned our way.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Reading the Sky
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the everyday motions of the Sun, Moon, stars and planets and the tides they cause.
levels.summary: Spin makes days, orbits make years and seasons, and the Moon’s orbit and gravity drive phases, eclipses and tides.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale. Everything in the sky moves for a reason.
cards.body: Sunrise, a wheeling sky, a looping Mars, the tide coming in. It can look like chaos up there. It's mostly a few simple motions, and you now know them.

cards.headline: Spin, orbit, pull
cards.body: Earth's spin gives day and night and sweeps the Sun and stars from east to west. Earth's orbit gives the year and a night sky that changes with the seasons. The Moon, circling us, brings phases, eclipses and, with its gravity, tides. And the planets wander along the ecliptic, with Mars looping back whenever Earth overtakes it. A few motions, one very busy sky.
cards.callout: Spin → day · Orbit → year · Moon → tides

cards.fact: Each star rises about 4 minutes earlier every night.
cards.context: Earth moves a little along its orbit each day, so each night the stars get a small head start. Four minutes is nothing on its own. But over a year those minutes add up to a whole different night sky, one season's constellations at a time.
